# Alliance Public Ownership and Economic Democracy Policy 2026 (PDF)

> Archive note: Uploaded 2026-10-02; linked from the matching policy post. Text extracted from the party's PDF with pdftotext; bullets normalised to Markdown, page breaks shown as horizontal rules; images/graphics not reproduced.

## Full text (verbatim)

Alliance Party of Aotearoa New Zealand

Alliance Public Ownership and Economic
Democracy Policy
Taking Control of Our Essential Infrastructure
The Alliance believes that the essential infrastructure of a modern nation should
serve the people who depend on it, not private shareholders seeking to maximise
profits.
The privatisation programme of the 1980s and 1990s transferred ownership and
control of important New Zealand assets away from the public. It fragmented
essential services, weakened democratic accountability, and allowed private and
overseas interests to gain control over infrastructure fundamental to our economic
and social wellbeing.
The Alliance will reverse this process.
We will protect the public assets that remain in public ownership, prevent further
privatisation and progressively return strategically important infrastructure to public
ownership.
Our objective is not state ownership for its own sake. It is to ensure that essential
services are affordable, reliable, environmentally sustainable, democratically
accountable, and operated in the public interest.

1. Public Ownership of Strategic Assets
The Alliance will establish a clear principle that strategic national infrastructure
should be publicly owned.
The immediate priority will be to protect existing public assets from privatisation and
identify assets that should be progressively returned to public ownership.
This will include consideration of:
- electricity generation, transmission, and distribution;
- ports and strategic transport infrastructure;
- water infrastructure;
- telecommunications infrastructure;
- other natural monopolies and essential services where private ownership
is inconsistent with the public interest.
The Alliance will establish a programme of reverse privatisation, progressively
purchasing strategic assets where necessary to restore democratic public
ownership.

1

---

Assets sold below their underlying public value, and assets where private ownership
has driven up the cost to consumers, will be the first priority for acquisition.
We will retain public ownership and ensure these assets operate as genuine public
services; with their success measured by the benefits they provide to New Zealand
rather than simply by commercial returns.

2. Stop Further Privatisation
There will be no further sale of strategic state assets.
The Alliance will prevent the sale, partial privatisation, or fragmentation of essential
public infrastructure.
We will also oppose arrangements that achieve privatisation by other means,
including:
- public-private partnerships where they transfer public assets or excessive
returns to private interests;
- contracting out essential public functions where this undermines
accountability;
- long-term concessions that effectively transfer public control;
- joint ventures designed primarily to introduce private ownership into
strategic infrastructure.
Public ownership must mean genuine public control, not simply government
retaining a minority share while private interests control the operation.

3. Electricity: Public Ownership and Affordable Power
Electricity is an essential service and a foundation of the modern economy.
The Alliance will re-integrate electricity generation, transmission, distribution, and
retail under public ownership and democratic control.
Our objectives will be:
- affordable electricity for households;
- reliable supply for businesses;
- secure national energy infrastructure;
- investment in renewable generation;
- improved energy efficiency;
- reduced energy poverty;
- long-term protection of New Zealand's energy security.
Electricity infrastructure should not be managed primarily as a vehicle for extracting
dividends from consumers.
Public ownership will allow investment decisions to be based on long-term national
need rather than short-term shareholder returns.

2

---

4. Ports and Strategic Transport Infrastructure
New Zealand's ports are critical national infrastructure.
The Alliance will progressively restore public ownership of strategically important
ports where they have been privatised or corporatised in ways that undermine public
control.
Ports should operate as part of an integrated national transport and economic
development strategy.
Public ownership will allow us to coordinate:
- ports;
- rail;
- coastal shipping;
- roads;
- regional development.
As a single system rather than allowing each part of the system to operate primarily
according to separate commercial interests.
The objective is an efficient national freight system that supports exporters, workers,
regional economies and consumers.

5. KiwiRail and Air New Zealand
Rail is in full public ownership. Air New Zealand is majority Crown-owned.
The Alliance will retain rail in full public ownership and will move Air New Zealand
from majority Crown control to full public ownership.
These assets should be operated in the national interest and integrated into wider
economic, transport, and regional development strategies.
Rail will play a central role in moving freight and passengers, while Air New Zealand
will provide an essential national and international transport connection.
Public ownership gives New Zealand the opportunity to make long-term decisions
about these services, without the requirement to maximise returns to private
shareholders.

3

---

6. Water Belongs to the People
Water is a fundamental public resource and must remain under public and
community control.
The Alliance will ensure that water services cannot be converted into private
profit-making utilities.
We will oppose:
- privatisation;
- commercialisation that places profit ahead of public need;
- contracting out essential water services;
- private control of strategic water infrastructure.
Water services will be managed through accountable public and community
institutions, with local communities having a meaningful role in decisions affecting
them.
Water is a public good, not a commodity.

7. Public Telecommunications and the Digital Commons
Modern telecommunications infrastructure is as important to New Zealand's
economy as roads, rail, and electricity.
The Alliance will return strategically important telecommunications infrastructure to
public ownership.
Particular priority will be given to infrastructure that functions as a natural
monopoly, including the essential “last mile” connecting households and
businesses.
The objective will be universal access to:
- affordable internet;
- reliable telecommunications;
- modern digital infrastructure;
- high-quality services regardless of geographic location.
No New Zealander should be excluded from full participation in society because they
live in a rural community or cannot afford essential communications services.

4

---

8. Public Ownership Must Be Democratic
Public ownership alone does not guarantee public control.
The Alliance will establish strong democratic accountability over publicly owned
enterprises.
Public enterprises will be required to:
- operate transparently;
- publish meaningful information about their operations;
- engage with workers and their unions;
- consult affected communities;
- be accountable to parliament and the public;
- pursue social and environmental as well as economic objectives.
State-owned enterprises are already subject to the Official Information Act. We will
extend it to publicly listed companies in which the Crown holds a controlling stake,
which currently sit outside it, and narrow the grounds for withholding access to
information across the entities already covered.
Community and regional representation will be strengthened in decisions affecting
essential services.

9. Workers Should Have a Voice in Public Enterprises
The people who work in public enterprises have an important role in ensuring those
enterprises operate effectively.
The Alliance will introduce stronger forms of workplace democracy, including:
- work councils in larger enterprises;
- worker representation on the boards of major public enterprises;
- meaningful consultation with unions;
- access to relevant information about the operation of public enterprises.
Workers should not be treated simply as a cost to be minimised.
They are participants in the operation of the enterprise and should have a genuine
voice in its future.

10. Public Ownership and the Environment
Public ownership provides an opportunity to make long-term environmental decisions
that private markets may not adequately recognise.
All publicly owned infrastructure will be required to operate within strong
environmental standards.
Investment decisions will take account of:

5

---

- climate change;
- biodiversity;
- resource conservation;
- energy efficiency;
- pollution;
- long-term sustainability.
The Alliance's economic policy will be guided by the principle that economic activity
must operate within the ecological limits of the natural world.
Strategic public ownership will therefore be used not only to improve affordability and
accountability, but also to support New Zealand's transition to a sustainable
economy.

11. Public Ownership and Regional Development
Strategic infrastructure should support every part of New Zealand, not simply the
areas offering the highest immediate commercial return. Our new ministry of works,
KiwiWorks, will be the vehicle for delivery of infrastructure in our country.
Public enterprises will be required to consider regional development as part of their
responsibilities.
Government will coordinate investment in:
- transport;
- energy;
- telecommunications;
- water;
- ports;
- regional infrastructure.
This will support employment, local businesses, and regional economic
development.
Economic development should ensure that the costs and benefits of development
are shared across all regions of New Zealand.

12. A Development Bank and National Development Strategy
Public ownership should form part of a wider economic strategy.
The Alliance will establish a Ministry of Development responsible for coordinating
national, regional, and community development.
The Ministry will develop a long-term New Zealand Development Strategy focused
on:
- full employment;
- productive investment;

6

---

- regional development;
- technological development;
- infrastructure;
- environmental sustainability;
- economic resilience.
A publicly owned Development Bank will provide concessional finance and venture
capital for productive investment, including cooperatives, young farmers, and
small-scale, appropriate technology projects.
This will ensure public ownership is complemented by public investment in the
productive economy.

13. Economic Democracy Rather Than Market Dominance
The Alliance believes the market should be a tool of economic policy, not the
master of it.
Where markets operate effectively and competitively, they can have a role.
But essential services and natural monopolies are different.
Where the public depends upon an infrastructure network for basic needs ­–
electricity, water, transport or communications ­– the overriding consideration must be
public benefit.
The Alliance will therefore reject the idea that everything should be bought, sold, and
managed according to commercial returns.
Economic policy should instead pursue:
- full employment;
- social wellbeing;
- regional development;
- environmental sustainability;
- democratic ownership.

14. A Fair Approach to Restoring Public Ownership
Returning assets to public ownership will require significant investment.
The Alliance will therefore develop a long-term public ownership programme,
prioritising assets according to:
- their strategic importance;
- their role as natural monopolies;
- their importance to essential services;
- the extent of private market failure;
- the cost to consumers;

7

---

- their importance to national security and resilience;
- their environmental significance;
- the feasibility and cost of acquisition.
Public ownership will be pursued progressively and responsibly rather than through
an arbitrary programme of acquisitions.
Where appropriate, the Crown will purchase assets at fair value, use existing public
investment vehicles, or establish new public entities to bring infrastructure under
public control.

15. Economic Resilience and the Protection of Critical Industries
The Alliance will develop a process by which the government identifies industries
and firms considered critical for reasons of national security, economic resilience,
local employment, and environmental stewardship.
In order to retain economic sovereignty, the government will have the ability to enact
a “first right of refusal” on the sale or liquidation of identified firms for the reasons
mentioned above, depending on fiscal viability. From there, the government may
facilitate transition to workers’ cooperatives or operate those businesses as a public
enterprise.
International markets operate in cycles of boom and bust, but as a small and
relatively isolated island nation, maintaining our strategic manufacturing and
industrial base at a level that can serve the domestic market in times of uncertainty is
critical.

Our Vision
The Alliance believes that the wealth and infrastructure of New Zealand should
work for New Zealanders.
We will protect the public ownership we have retained, including rail and the Crown's
majority holding in Air New Zealand, and progressively restore public ownership of
other strategic assets that were sold.
We will return to public ownership of:
- electricity generation and distribution;
- ports;
- water and telecommunications infrastructure.
We will build a system in which public enterprises are not simply government-owned
corporations operating according to private-sector principles, but democratically
accountable public institutions with social, economic, and environmental
responsibilities.
The Alliance's vision is an economy in which:

8

---

- essential services are publicly owned;
- strategic infrastructure is democratically controlled;
- workers have a voice;
- communities have a say;
- profits do not determine access to basic necessities;
- investment serves long-term national interests;
- and economic development operates within environmental limits.
Public ownership is not an end in itself. It is the means by which New Zealanders
can regain democratic control over the infrastructure on which our collective future
depends.

9

## Full text (verbatim)

Alliance Party of Aotearoa New Zealand

Alliance Retirement and Aged-Care Policy
Security, Dignity, and Independence in Later Life
Our Vision
The Alliance believes that every person has the right to security, dignity, and
independence in later life.
Retirement income and aged care are not privileges to be provided according to a
person's wealth. They are essential components of a just society and should be
available as universal rights.
The Alliance will defend the universal pension, raise it to a level people can live on, and
provide high-quality public services and care based on need later in life, rather than by
ability to pay.
Our retirement and aged-care policies will recognise the contribution older people have
made to society, and ensure that no one is forced into poverty, insecurity, or inadequate
care because they have reached retirement age or require long-term support.

1. A Universal Right to Retirement Income
The Alliance will maintain a universal state pension as a fundamental social right.
Entitlement will be based on age and residency, rather than income or wealth. The state
pension will not be means-tested.
The Alliance will:
- maintain the age of entitlement for the pension at 65, with no intention of raising it
at any point;
- maintain universal eligibility for people who meet the appropriate age and
residency requirements;
- ensure that retirement income provides genuine economic security, rather than
merely preventing destitution;
- recognise the state pension as a universal entitlement and an essential part of
Aotearoa New Zealand's social security system.
Retirement should be a time when people can live with security and dignity, regardless
of their personal wealth. Maintaining the age of the pension at sixty-five is a red line for
the Alliance, and we see the merit of an argument for lowering it rather than raising it
over time. Ordinary working people have been largely shut out of significant productivity

1

---

gains over many decades, and we intend to reverse that trend by investing in an
increase in meaningful free time for all.

2. An Adequate and Secure State Pension
The level of the state pension must allow older people to participate fully in society and
maintain a reasonable standard of living.
The Alliance will increase the married rate of New Zealand Superannuation to 72.5
percent of the after-tax average wage.
The pension will be:
- funded from general taxation;
- adjusted regularly to reflect movements in both wages and the cost of living.
The Alliance opposes any move to reintroduce a superannuation surcharge or to
impose means-testing on the state pension. Retirement income should remain a
universal entitlement based on age and residency, rather than being reduced or
withdrawn because an older person has other income, savings, or assets.
A universal pension recognises that retirement security is a collective social
responsibility and that people should be able to plan for their retirement with confidence
and certainty.

3. Protecting Retirement Income from Inflation
Older people are particularly vulnerable to increases in the cost of essential goods and
services because many rely on fixed or relatively predictable incomes.
The Alliance will therefore provide strong and automatic protection for the purchasing
power of retirement incomes.
State pensions will be adjusted quarterly in response to movements in average
earnings or the Consumer Price Index, whichever is greater.
Pension rates will also maintain their relationship with average weekly earnings,
ensuring that older people’s living standards do not fall progressively behind those of
working Kiwis.
Indexation will be automatic rather than dependent on governments, making
discretionary decisions about whether pensioners can afford to keep pace with rising
costs.

4. Universal and Dignified Aged Care
The need for residential or long-term care should not result in older people having to
exhaust their lifetime savings before receiving proper support.

2

---

The Alliance will abolish means-testing for older people requiring long-term
hospital or residential care.
Access to appropriate care will be based on need rather than wealth.
We will provide:
- high-quality residential and hospital care;
- appropriate assessment, rehabilitation, and support services;
- safe and dignified environments for older people; and
- appropriate support for people to remain independent in their own homes
wherever possible.
Public funding for aged care must be directed towards care, rather than private profit.

5. Protecting Aged-Care Workers and the Quality of Care
The quality of care provided to older people depends upon the people who provide that
care.
The Alliance will ensure that public funding for elderly assessment, rehabilitation, and
care is appropriately directed towards:
- adequate staffing;
- fair wages and employment conditions;
- manageable workloads;
- training and professional development; and
- safe staffing levels and quality care.
Public funding must not be used to subsidise inadequate staffing, unmanageable
workloads, or the extraction of profits from essential aged-care services.
Where public money is provided to private or community providers, there must be
strong accountability to ensure that funding delivers high-quality care and decent
employment conditions.

6. Transport, Communications, and Social Connection
Financial security alone is not sufficient to ensure a dignified retirement.
Older people must be able to remain connected to their communities and participate
fully in society.
The Alliance will provide older people with:
- free or subsidised public transport;

3

---

- subsidised telephone and internet connections;
- access to essential communication services; and
- support for community-based services that reduce isolation and enable older
people to remain active, independent, and empowered to continue living in their
own homes for as long as possible.
We recognise that access to transport and communications is particularly important for
older people living alone, living in rural communities, or with limited mobility.
No older person should be isolated from their family, community, or essential services
because they cannot afford to travel or communicate.

7. Independent Advocacy for Older People
Older people must have a strong and independent voice when dealing with government
agencies, health services, aged-care providers, and other institutions.
The Alliance will establish and fund independent advocacy services for older
people.
These services will:
- provide independent advice and assistance;
- support older people to understand and exercise their rights;
- assist people who experience inadequate or inappropriate care;
- advocate for older people in dealings with government and service providers; and
- identify systemic problems affecting older people and bring them to the attention
of government.
Advocacy services must be independent of the organisations whose decisions they may
be required to challenge.

8. A Ministry for Senior Citizens
The Alliance will establish a dedicated Ministry for Senior Citizens.
The Ministry will ensure that the interests and needs of older people are properly
considered across the whole of government.
Its responsibilities will include:
- monitoring the impact of government policies on older people;
- advising Cabinet and government agencies on the economic and social position
of senior citizens;
- developing targeted social and economic programmes;

4

---

- monitoring retirement income adequacy;
- overseeing the effectiveness of services for older people;
- supporting independent advocacy; and
- consulting regularly with senior citizens and organisations representing them.
The needs of older people should not be an afterthought within government policy. A
dedicated Ministry will ensure that their interests have a permanent and authoritative
voice within government.

9. Future Proofing with KiwiSaver and an Adequate Super Scheme
Aotearoa New Zealand was robbed of an opportunity to build a Superannuation Fund
worth more than a trillion dollars, due to the repeal of the Superannuation Act (1974).
The Alliance Party believes that moving towards a similar policy is possible through
steady reform and greater investment in KiwiSaver.
We will immediately establish an automatic $10,000 endowment for all new KiwiSaver
accounts, ring-fenced until retirement or terminal illness. This will provide enough of an
initial boost to effectively leverage KiwiSaver into a meaningful, long-term savings
scheme.
We will phase out the use of “active” KiwiSaver funds, with investment directed into
passive funds that are focused on local infrastructure and investment. Working Kiwis
should not have to worry about how and where their retirement fund is being invested,
as a dignified and well-resourced retirement is a net social good.

10. Security, Dignity, and Independence
The Alliance's retirement and aged-care policies are based on a simple principle:
growing older should never mean losing economic security, dignity, or independence.
A universal state pension will provide a secure foundation for retirement. Adequate
indexation will protect pensioners from inflation and declining living standards. Universal
access to long-term care will ensure that people are not required to impoverish
themselves to receive necessary support.
The KiwiSaver endowment gives everyone a stake in a fund with up to sixty-five years
to grow and requires that a meaningful share of it is invested here. Our retirement
savings currently do a great deal of work for economies other than our own. Directed
into local infrastructure and productive industry, the same money builds the country that
people are saving to retire in, while also lifting the wealth floor for the working Kiwi.
At the same time, better aged-care staffing, subsidised transport and communications,
independent advocacy, and a dedicated Ministry for Senior Citizens will ensure that
older people are able to remain connected, respected, and active members of society.

5

---

The Alliance will build a retirement and aged-care system based on universal rights
rather than means testing, dignity rather than dependence, and public responsibility
rather than private profit.
Older people have contributed throughout their working and community lives to building
Aotearoa New Zealand. They are entitled to security and dignity in return.

6

# Small Business, Local Enterprise, and Cooperative Development (PDF)

> Archive note: Uploaded 2026-09-18; linked from the matching policy post. Text extracted from the party's PDF with pdftotext; bullets normalised to Markdown, page breaks shown as horizontal rules; images/graphics not reproduced.

## Full text (verbatim)

Alliance Party of Aotearoa New Zealand

Small Business, Local Enterprise, and
Cooperative Development
Our Vision
The Alliance believes that small businesses, family enterprises, farmers,
self-employed people, cooperatives, and locally owned enterprises are an essential
part of a strong and democratic economy. They provide employment, sustain
communities, and keep economic wealth circulating locally.

Small operators should not be expected to compete on unequal terms with large
corporations, banks, and financial institutions. Government has a responsibility to
protect smaller enterprises from excessive market power while providing them with
the finance, skills, technology, and infrastructure needed to succeed.

1. Protecting Small and Family Businesses
The Alliance will ensure that taxation and economic policy do not place unnecessary
burdens on small businesses, family enterprises, small farmers, and other
small-scale operators.

Where taxes on land, commercial property, or other assets are introduced to address
excessive concentration of wealth and ownership, appropriate thresholds and
exemptions will ensure that genuinely small businesses, owner-operators, and family
farms are not unfairly penalised.

The objective will be to ensure that taxation falls principally on accumulated wealth
and large-scale ownership, rather than on the productive activity of small enterprises.

2. Challenging Corporate Concentration and Monopoly Power
The Alliance recognises that small businesses and self-employed people can be
exploited by large corporations, banks, and financial institutions through excessive

1

---

prices, restrictive contracts, access to finance, supply-chain control, and unequal
bargaining power.

The Commerce Commission has estimated that the supermarket duopoly takes
around $430 million a year in excess profits. A supplier dealing with two buyers has
no meaningful ability to negotiate, and neither does a small retailer competing
against them.

The Alliance will strengthen competition law and act against concentration and
monopoly power so that smaller operators have genuine access to markets and are
not forced into unfair relationships with dominant firms.

Small business owners, farmers, contractors, and wage earners share an interest in
an economy that prevents the concentration of economic power in the hands of a
small number of corporations and financial institutions.

3. A Public Development Finance System
The Alliance will establish and strengthen public development finance to provide
affordable capital to small businesses, farmers, cooperatives, community
enterprises, and new ventures that are unable to obtain appropriate finance from
commercial institutions.

A publicly owned Development Bank will provide concessional, low-interest finance
for productive investment, including for young farmers, agricultural cooperatives,
small businesses, and locally owned enterprises.

Access to public finance will be directed towards productive economic activity,
employment, innovation, and regional development rather than speculative
investment.

Government-backed venture capital will be available for small-scale individual and
group enterprise, particularly where it creates lasting employment or meets local
economic and community needs.

2

---

4. Supporting Self-Employment and New Enterprises
The Alliance will actively support people seeking to establish viable small
businesses, cooperatives, and self-employment initiatives.

Employment and enterprise resource centres will provide practical assistance,
including business planning, financial management, training, employment advice,
and access to government development programmes.

The purpose will be to give people the practical means to establish and sustain
enterprises, rather than simply expecting individuals to succeed without access to
capital, knowledge, or support.

5. Building Locally Owned Technology and Innovation
The Alliance will support the development and adoption of appropriate technology by
locally owned businesses.

An Applied Technology Programme will provide advice, technical assistance, and
venture capital for technology-based projects, with particular emphasis on
small-scale and appropriate technology that contributes to the wider national
development strategy.

A publicly supported technology advisory service will be available to locally owned
companies, ensuring that small and medium-sized enterprises can access
technological expertise that would otherwise be beyond their means.

6. Supporting Cooperatives and Local Ownership
Cooperatives provide an alternative to concentrated corporate ownership by allowing
producers, workers, consumers, and communities to share ownership and
decision-making.

Public development finance will give particular weight to cooperative ventures,
including agricultural cooperatives and enterprises that retain economic value within
local communities, with particular guidance for businesses that would otherwise shut
down being bought out and turned into a cooperative by their employees.

3

---

Government procurement and development programmes should, wherever practical,
support locally owned and locally based enterprises.

7. Linking Small Business Policy to Regional Development
Small business policy will form part of a wider national and regional development
strategy.
Government will work with local communities, councils, workers, farmers,
businesses, and cooperatives to identify opportunities for sustainable regional
economic development.

Investment will support local employment, value-added production, innovation,
infrastructure, and training. Particular attention will be given to regions where
economic restructuring or the decline of major employers has weakened local
economies.

The Alliance's objective is not simply to create more small businesses, but to build
strong local economies in which locally owned enterprises can thrive.
8. Training and Skills for Enterprise
Access to appropriate skills and training is essential to the success of small
enterprises.

The Alliance will expand access to business, technical, and vocational training,
including through Employment Resource Centres and other publicly supported
programmes.

Training will be linked to regional development strategies and emerging industries so
that workers and small businesses have the skills required to take advantage of new
economic opportunities.

9. A Fairer Relationship Between Small Business and the State
Government regulation should protect workers, consumers, and the environment
while avoiding unnecessary administrative burdens on genuinely small enterprises.

4

---

The Alliance will work with small businesses and their representative organisations
to ensure that regulatory systems are proportionate and practical.

Small-business status must not be used as a means of avoiding employment rights,
health and safety obligations, environmental standards, or taxation. Where a person
is a worker in substance, they should be a worker in law, whatever the contract says.
Alliance workers’ rights policy extends minimum employment protections to
contractors for that reason, and genuine small enterprise has nothing to fear from it.

The businesses undercut by misclassification are overwhelmingly other small
businesses, competing against operators who are not paying holiday pay.

10. Getting Paid on Time
Late payments are one of the most common causes of small business failure. A firm
can be profitable on paper and still go under waiting for money it has already earned.

The Alliance will:

- legislate maximum payment terms for large firms and public agencies
contracting with small businesses;
- require interest to accrue automatically on overdue commercial invoices,
without the smaller party having to ask;
- require large firms to publish their average payment times;
- ensure public agencies meet their own payment terms and report against
them.

A small business should not be providing an interest-free loan to a company many
times its size.

11. Small Enterprise as Part of a Democratic Economy
We do not believe that economic policy should simply maximise the number or size
of private businesses. Nor do we believe that small businesses should be left to
compete against increasingly concentrated corporate and financial power without
assistance.

5

---

The Alliance will build an economic system in which small businesses, workers,
farmers, cooperatives, communities, and publicly owned enterprises can operate
alongside one another, with the government providing the finance, infrastructure,
skills, and regulatory framework necessary to ensure that economic power is widely
distributed.

The objective is an economy in which enterprise serves people and communities,
wealth is retained within Aotearoa New Zealand, productive investment is
encouraged, and economic development contributes to decent employment, regional
prosperity, and social wellbeing.

6

# Alliance Tax Justice and Cost of Living Policy 2026 (PDF)

> Archive note: Uploaded 2026-09-06; linked from the matching policy post. Text extracted from the party's PDF with pdftotext; bullets normalised to Markdown, page breaks shown as horizontal rules; images/graphics not reproduced.

## Full text (verbatim)

Alliance Party of Aotearoa New Zealand

Alliance Tax Justice and Cost of Living
Policy
A Fair Tax System and Real Relief for Working People
The Alliance believes that the essentials of living a good life should be readily
accessible to all.
Our country taxes income from the very first dollar earned. Not from the first dollar a
person can spare, and not from the point at which they are getting ahead, but from the
money that pays for food, power, and rent.
At the same time, wealth that grows without work is taxed lightly, occasionally, or not at
all.
The Alliance rejects the idea that a fair tax system is one which asks the most of those
with the least.
We will shift the burden of taxation away from wages and salaries and onto wealth, and
we will use the proceeds to deliver permanent, universal cost of living relief to every
person in Aotearoa New Zealand.

1. A Tax-Free Threshold of $20,000
The Alliance will make the first $20,000 of every person's income completely tax
free.
The threshold will be:

- universal, applying to every income earner regardless of occupation, employment
status, or level of income;
- automatic, delivered through the pay system rather than by application, means test,
or annual claim;
- equal in value, returning the same amount to every person who earns above it;
- permanent, forming a standing feature of the tax system rather than a temporary
package; and
- reviewed over time, so that its value is not eroded by inflation.
Because the relief is drawn from the bottom of the income scale, every person's income
passes through it. The cleaner and the surgeon receive exactly the same benefit.
This is deliberate. A universal threshold creates a shared entitlement, rather than a
targeted concession, and it cannot be withdrawn as a person's circumstances change.

1

---

2. Why the Burden Has Fallen on Wages
The current imbalance in taxation is not an accident, and it is not a loophole; it is
designed this way.
Income earned through work is taxed at source, every pay, automatically. A wage earner
has no opportunity to arrange matters otherwise, and no realistic ability to defer,
restructure, or relocate their income.
Income and wealth accumulated through property ownership and investments are treated
differently. Much of it is not taxed as it accrues, and some of it is not taxed at all.
Inland Revenue's own research into the wealthiest families found that they pay a
substantially lower effective rate on their economic income than an ordinary wage and
salary earner does. This is not a claim advanced by the Alliance. It is the finding of the
tax department itself.
A tax system which leans this heavily on wages is a political choice. A different
choice can be made.

3. A Capital Gains Tax
Aotearoa New Zealand is one of very few developed countries without a broad tax on
capital gains.
The Alliance will introduce a broad-based capital gains tax, covering investment
property, shares, and business assets.
The family home will be excluded. This is not a tax on the house people live in.
The principle is straightforward. When a person earns money by working, they pay tax on
it. When a person makes a gain from an asset, in most cases, they do not. There is no
principled reason for treating the two differently.
The Alliance will also be clear about how this tax behaves. A capital gains tax applies
only to gains that accrue after it begins and only when an asset is sold. It builds gradually
towards its full value over a number of years. It is a durable, long-term revenue base, not
an immediate windfall, and we will not present it as one.

4. A Tax on Very Large Accumulations of Wealth
The Alliance will introduce an annual tax on net wealth above a high threshold of $2
million, together with a companion tax on assets held in trusts.
The trust provision is essential rather than incidental. This country has hundreds of
thousands of trusts. A wealth tax without a trust tax could be arranged around by anyone
with an accountant and would raise a fraction of what is claimed for it.
This measure will affect a very small number of people.
It is not directed at families who have paid off a mortgage over a working lifetime.
Instead, it focuses on wealth held by those at the very top, which has grown steadily over
four decades while wages have not kept pace.

2

---

The Alliance will properly resource Inland Revenue to administer and enforce these
measures. A tax which is legislated but not collected achieves nothing.

5. A Financial Transactions Tax
The Alliance will introduce a very small levy on financial market transactions,
including share trading, currency dealing, and derivatives.
The levy will not apply to the ordinary financial life of households. It will not apply to:
- wages and salaries being paid;
- mortgage or rent payments;
- household bills and everyday purchases; or
- KiwiSaver and other retirement savings contributions.
This is a levy on the churn of the financial sector, not on the ordinary business of having a
bank account.
The Alliance will design this measure conservatively. Other countries have introduced
transactions taxes and seen trading activity relocate offshore. A low rate applied to a
clearly defined domestic base is more likely to raise a reliable sum than an ambitious rate
applied to activity that can simply move.

6. Rebalancing the Income Tax Scale
The remaining revenue comes from the shape of the income tax scale itself.
Our tax scale currently flattens out well below the level of genuinely high incomes. A
person on a middling professional salary and a person earning several hundred thousand
dollars contribute at rates far closer together than most people assume.
The Alliance will:
- extend the upper rates further down the range of genuinely high incomes;
- introduce a new top rate above them; and
- leave the rates applying to low and middle incomes unchanged or reduced.
Under this policy the overwhelming majority will pay less income tax than they do
today. Those who pay more are concentrated among the highest earners in the country.

7. What This Policy Does Not Claim
The Alliance believes political parties should be plain about the limits of their own
proposals.
This is a tax policy, not a complete fiscal plan. Our commitments on health, housing,
and infrastructure are developed and cost determined separately, and this policy does not
purport to fund them in full.
This is not an attack on people who have done well. A person who has built a
business, worked long hours, and become comfortable has done nothing wrong. What
the Alliance challenges is a structure which asks less of income derived from ownership
than it asks of income derived from work.

3

---

This is not a promise that no one will pay more. Some people will, and they are
concentrated at the top of the income and wealth distribution. A rebalancing means
moving weight from one place to another.

8. Our Commitment
The Alliance will make the first $20,000 of every person's income tax free, funded
through a broad capital gains tax, a tax on very large wealth, a levy on financial market
transactions, and a rebalancing of the income tax scale.
We believe that:
- the money people need to live on should not be taxed;

- wealth that accumulates through ownership rather than effort should be
taxed;

- relief should be universal, not rationed;

- a tax system should ask most of those best able to contribute.

This policy is a practical expression of a simple principle: an economy should serve the
people who do the work to make it possible.

4

# Alliance Te Tiriti o Waitangi, Democracy, and Constitutional Policy 2026 (PDF)

> Archive note: Uploaded 2026-09-26; linked from the matching policy post. Text extracted from the party's PDF with pdftotext; bullets normalised to Markdown, page breaks shown as horizontal rules; images/graphics not reproduced.

## Full text (verbatim)

Alliance Party of Aotearoa New Zealand

Te Tiriti o Waitangi, Democracy, and
Constitutional Policy
Democracy, Sovereignty, and the Power of the People
The Alliance believes that democracy must mean more than voting every three
years.
A genuinely democratic society is one in which people have a meaningful ability to
shape the decisions that affect their lives, their communities, and their future.
Political power must not be concentrated in the hands of governments, multinational
corporations, wealthy individuals, or distant bureaucracies. It must be accountable to
the people.
The Alliance seeks to build a participatory democracy in which decisions are made
as close as practicable to the people affected by them, while maintaining national
institutions capable of ensuring equality, social justice, and the protection of national
interests.
Democratic government must extend into economic and social life. Political
democracy is weakened when economic power is concentrated in a small number of
private hands.
Our constitutional policy is therefore founded on four principles:
- Popular sovereignty: political authority ultimately belongs to the people.
- Participatory democracy: people and communities must have meaningful
control over decisions affecting them.
- Social justice: democracy must protect equality, human rights, and the
dignity of every person.
- Upholding Te Tiriti o Waitangi: the constitutional relationship between
tangata whenua and the wider population of Aotearoa must be honoured and
strengthened.

1. Te Tiriti o Waitangi: The Constitutional Foundation
The Alliance recognises Te Tiriti o Waitangi as the foundational constitutional
document of Aotearoa.
In particular, the Māori text of Te Tiriti o Waitangi must be recognised as the primary
expression of the agreement entered into between Māori and the Crown.

1

---

A just democratic society cannot be built upon the dispossession or marginalisation
of tangata whenua.
The Alliance therefore rejects institutional racism and supports constitutional
arrangements that recognise mana motuhake and the distinct rights, interests, and
responsibilities of Māori, while ensuring a democratic society based on cooperation
and mutual respect.
The relationship established by Te Tiriti o Waitangi must be reflected throughout the
machinery of government, legislation, and public decision-making.

Te Tiriti o Waitangi Obligations
The Crown must honour its obligations under Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
This includes:
- recognising Māori participation in constitutional and governmental
decision-making;
- protecting Māori rights and interests;
- addressing the consequences of historical Crown breaches;
- eliminating institutional discrimination; and
- ensuring that public institutions operate consistently with the principles of Te
Tiriti o Waitangi.
Honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi is not simply a matter of consultation. It must be
reflected in the structure and operation of the state.

2. Waitangi Tribunal and Historical Grievances
The Alliance will strengthen the Waitangi Tribunal and ensure that it has the
resources and independence necessary to perform its constitutional role effectively.
Māori must have a meaningful role in the appointment of Māori members of the
Tribunal, including consideration of mechanisms through which iwi can directly select
or nominate those members.
The Government will commit to acting upon the recommendations of the Waitangi
Tribunal relating to Treaty breaches, environmental resources, and other matters
within its jurisdiction.
Historical grievances must be addressed fairly and transparently.
The purpose of Treaty settlement is not simply to rectify historical breaches, but to
establish a durable constitutional relationship for the future.

2

---

3. Participatory and Community Democracy
The Alliance will decentralise political power wherever practicable.
Decisions should be made at the lowest effective level, provided that
decentralisation does not undermine equality, universal rights, or the ability of central
government to protect the public interest.
Local communities should have genuine control over matters that directly affect
them.
We will strengthen:
- local democratic institutions;
- community participation in public decision-making;
- public consultation and deliberation;
- community ownership of essential assets and services;
- mechanisms for direct citizen participation; and
- accountability of elected representatives to the communities they represent.
The Alliance rejects the idea that citizens should participate in democracy only by
casting a vote at election time.

4. A Proportional and Representative Parliament
The Alliance supports the continuation of Mixed Member Proportional
representation (MMP) as the basis of parliamentary democracy.
Parliament should reflect the diversity of political opinion within Aotearoa, rather than
artificially concentrating power in the hands of parties that receive only a minority of
the popular vote.
MMP will be protected and strengthened.

The Party Vote Threshold
The current party vote threshold is 5 percent, which is among the highest of any
proportional system. A party can be the choice of one voter in twenty and receive
nothing.
Two independent reviews have found the threshold higher than it needs to be. The
Electoral Commission's 2012 review of MMP recommended lowering it to 4 percent.
The Independent Electoral Review recommended 3.5 percent in its 2023 final report,
concluding that a lower threshold would broaden representation while still allowing
stable parliaments to form. Neither recommendation has been implemented.

3

---

The Alliance will lower the party vote threshold to 3.5 percent, in line with the most
recent independent recommendation. Over time, we believe that the removal of the
threshold and a simple percentage for each seat is the most democratic option, and
will represent the implementation of a proportional system reaching maturity.
A threshold set high enough to discard one voter in twenty is protecting incumbents
rather than stability.
Any future changes to the electoral system must preserve the fundamental principles
of proportionality, representation, and political pluralism.

5. Strengthening Parliament
Parliament must be an effective check on executive power.
The Alliance will strengthen the ability of parliament and its select committees to
scrutinise government decisions, public expenditure, and the performance of
government agencies.
Government budgets should be accompanied by independent assessments of their:
- social impacts;
- economic impacts;
- environmental impacts; and
- distributional consequences.
Select committees will be strengthened so that they can properly question ministers,
officials, and public agencies.
Officials should be required to provide parliament with accurate and comprehensive
information, subject to legitimate protections for privacy, national security, and other
clearly defined public interests.

6. Reforming Cabinet Government
The Alliance will reform the conventions surrounding cabinet collective
responsibility.
Ministers should not be prevented from expressing disagreement with government
policies, or from participating openly in parliamentary debate.
Collective responsibility should operate where necessary to ensure coherent
government, but it should not become a mechanism for suppressing legitimate
political debate or preventing parliament from properly scrutinising government
decisions.
Greater transparency within government will strengthen rather than weaken
democratic government.

4

---

7. A Written Constitution
New Zealand's constitutional arrangements have developed through legislation,
convention, judicial decisions, and historical practice.
The Alliance will initiate a comprehensive constitutional review to examine
whether Aotearoa should adopt a formal written constitution.
The review will be nationwide, participatory, and transparent to build a constitution
democratically from the ground up.
It should consider:
- the constitutional status of Te Tiriti o Waitangi;
- the recommendations of the Matike Mai report;
- the rights and responsibilities of citizens;
- the relationship between parliament, the executive, and the judiciary;
- the powers and limitations of government;
- the role of local government;
- the protection of democratic rights;
- mechanisms for constitutional amendment; and
- appropriate checks and balances on state power.
Any proposed written constitution must emerge from a genuine public process,
rather than being imposed by one government or political party.

8. Reviewing the Structure of Parliament
As part of the constitutional review, the Alliance will examine whether the present
structure of parliament provides the best possible system of democratic
representation and accountability.
This review will consider the possible establishment of a second legislative
chamber, including its purpose, composition, powers, and democratic legitimacy.
A second chamber is only worth having if it improves scrutiny. An appointed house of
former ministers would not achieve this.
The review will also consider appropriate mechanisms for ensuring regional,
community, and other forms of representation are properly reflected within the
constitutional system.

5

---

9. Citizens’ Initiatives
The Alliance supports greater opportunities for citizens to directly participate in the
legislative process.
The constitutional review will examine the establishment of Citizens’ Initiatives,
allowing citizens to propose legislative or policy changes through an appropriate
democratic process.
Any such system will include safeguards to ensure:
- adequate public information;
- meaningful debate;
- protection of minority and individual rights;
- clear and workable questions; and
- democratic legitimacy.
Direct democracy should complement representative democracy rather than replace
it.

10. The Future of the Monarchy
The Alliance believes that the constitutional status of the Crown should be subject to
democratic consideration.
As part of the national constitutional review, the people of Aotearoa should have the
opportunity to determine the future constitutional relationship between Aotearoa New
Zealand and the monarchy.
The Alliance therefore supports consideration of a referendum on the future of the
monarchy as part of a wider constitutional process.
Any constitutional change should be determined democratically by the people of
Aotearoa New Zealand.

11. Open and Transparent Government
Democracy cannot function effectively when citizens are denied access to
information about decisions made in their name.
The Alliance will strengthen the principle that government information belongs to
the public, subject only to clearly justified exceptions.
The Official Information Act will be extended to cover publicly listed companies in
which the Crown holds a controlling stake, which currently sit outside it, and the
grounds for withholding will be narrowed across the entities already covered.
Public information should be:

6

---

- freely accessible;
- provided promptly;
- available in understandable forms;
- proactively released wherever possible; and
- withheld only where there is a compelling and legally recognised reason.
The burden should be on government to justify secrecy, not on citizens to justify their
right to know.

12. Political Integrity and Conflicts of Interest
Public office exists to serve the public.
The Alliance will introduce stronger requirements to prevent conflicts of interest and
the undue influence of private wealth over political decision-making.
Candidates for public office will be required to publicly disclose relevant financial
interests and assets.
Elected representatives and senior public officials will be subject to clear and
enforceable conflict-of-interest rules.
The objective is not to prevent people with legitimate business, professional, or
community interests from entering politics. It is to ensure that those interests are
transparent and cannot secretly influence public decisions.

13. Political Donations and Democratic Equality
Political influence must not be determined by the ability to make large financial
contributions.
The Alliance will establish strict transparency requirements for political donations.
All significant individual and corporate donations to political parties will be publicly
disclosed.
The Alliance will also consider appropriate limits on political donations to prevent
wealthy individuals, corporations, and other organisations from acquiring
disproportionate political influence.
Political parties must be accountable for the sources of their funding.
The democratic process should be based on equal political citizenship, not the
financial power of particular interests.

14. Democracy and Economic Power
Political democracy cannot be separated from economic democracy.

7

---

A society in which a small number of corporations control essential infrastructure,
natural resources, employment, and investment cannot provide genuine democratic
control simply by holding regular elections.
The Alliance will therefore pursue democratic control of essential economic
resources through:
- public ownership;
- cooperative ownership;
- community ownership;
- worker participation;
- strong trade union rights; and
- democratic economic planning.
This principle connects our constitutional policy with our economic, environmental,
and social policies.
The people must have the power to determine the direction of society, rather than
being subordinate to the decisions of concentrated private economic power.

15. Democracy, Environment, and Future Generations
Democratic government has a responsibility not only to those who can vote today,
but also to future generations.
Environmental decisions must therefore be subject to democratic scrutiny and
long-term assessment.
Communities and tangata whenua must have a meaningful role in decisions
concerning:
- land;
- water;
- forests;
- minerals;
- energy;
- biodiversity; and
- other natural resources.
Environmental democracy and stewardship means that decisions affecting the
commons cannot be left solely to corporations, private investors, or central
government agencies.

8

---

This principle reinforces the Alliance commitment to public and community control of
essential resources, and to the protection of the natural environment for future
generations.

16. A Democratic Constitution for Aotearoa
The Alliance's constitutional vision is ultimately about where power resides.
We reject a political system in which citizens are expected to hand their democratic
authority to governments every three years and then have little meaningful influence
over the decisions that follow.
We seek a society in which:
- parliament represents the people proportionally;
- government is transparent and accountable;
- representatives are subject to recall by democratic means;
- communities have genuine democratic power;
- tangata whenua exercise their constitutional rights under Te Tiriti o Waitangi;
- citizens can participate directly in important decisions;
- political influence is not determined by wealth;
- public resources are protected from private exploitation; and
- economic power is subject to democratic control.
The Alliance will work towards a constitutional system that reflects the character of
Aotearoa as a democratic, diverse, and Treaty-based nation.
Our goal is not simply a better government. It is a more democratic society, but
one in which power is placed in the hands of the people and exercised in the
interests of all.

9

documents/pdf-trade-policy.md.text:
# Alliance Trade Policy 2026 (PDF)

> Archive note: Uploaded 2026-09-28; linked from the matching policy post. Text extracted from the party's PDF with pdftotext; bullets normalised to Markdown, page breaks shown as horizontal rules; images/graphics not reproduced.

## Full text (verbatim)

Alliance Party of Aotearoa New Zealand

Alliance Trade Policy
Trade That Serves Aotearoa New Zealand
The Alliance believes international trade should serve the interests of people,
communities, and the Aotearoa New Zealand economy rather than placing the
interests of multinational corporations above democratic decision-making.
Aotearoa New Zealand must retain the sovereign right to determine its own
economic, social, environmental, and employment policies.
The Alliance does not oppose international trade. Our country is a small country at
the end of a long supply line, and roughly a quarter of our economic activity currently
depends on selling to the world. What we oppose is a trade policy that treats market
access as worth any price, including the right to govern ourselves.

1. Economic Sovereignty
Political independence requires economic independence.
The Alliance will oppose international trade agreements and institutions where they
restrict the ability of democratically elected governments to:
- regulate the country's economy;
- protect workers and employment;
- protect the environment;
- regulate corporations;
- maintain public ownership;
- provide essential public services.
We must retain democratic control over essential services and strategic assets,
including:
- water;
- electricity;
- transport;
- telecommunications;
- health and other public services.
Trade agreements must never be allowed to force the privatisation or foreign
ownership of essential public services.

1

---

2. Trade That Protects Jobs and Living Standards
Trade policy will be designed to support decent employment and a productive
domestic economy.
The Alliance will use trade policy to:
- protect decent employment;
- support local manufacturing;
- encourage value-added domestic production;
- support regional economic development;
- protect health and safety standards;
- protect environmental standards;
- prevent exploitation of workers.
We must retain the ability to use tariffs and other trade measures to protect
strategic industries, domestic employment, and economic resilience.
Tariffs are a measure to be used sparingly, due to the impact on the price of goods
and the risk of retaliation against local exporters. They still have a role to play in
protecting local manufacturing and industry from the global race to the bottom.
Particular consideration will be given to industries vulnerable to unfair competition
based on exploitative wages and working conditions overseas.

3. No Race to the Bottom
International competition must not become a mechanism for driving down wages,
working conditions, or environmental standards.
The Alliance will oppose trade arrangements that encourage businesses to move
production to countries where workers can be paid poverty wages or where
environmental protections are inadequate.
Imported products should be required to meet appropriate labour, environmental,
health-and-safety standards comparable to those we require of our own producers.
Aotearoa New Zealand should have the right to determine those standards
democratically and to enforce them effectively.
International trade should raise living standards rather than drive a race to the
bottom in wages, working conditions, and environmental protection.

4. Protecting Democratic Government
Trade agreements must not give multinational corporations rights that override the
decisions of elected governments.
The Alliance will oppose trade arrangements that:
- undermine New Zealand's ability to regulate corporations;

2

---

- restrict legitimate public-interest legislation;
- prevent governments from protecting workers;
- undermine environmental regulation;
- limit public ownership;
- allow private commercial interests to challenge legitimate democratic
decisions.
No trade agreement should place corporate rights above democratic rights. The
Alliance will not sign an agreement containing investor­–state dispute settlement, and
will seek to remove it from those we are already party to. Aotearoa New Zealand has
already negotiated side letters curbing compulsory ISDS with five CPTPP partners,
which shows this can be done without leaving an agreement.

5. Supporting New Zealand Production
Trade policy must form part of a broader economic development strategy.
The Alliance will use appropriate trade and economic measures to strengthen New
Zealand's productive capacity, including support for:
- manufacturing;
- agriculture and food production;
- locally owned businesses;
- cooperatives;
- regional industries;
- technology and innovation;
- value-added exports.
The objective is not simply to export more commodities. It is a productive,
diversified, and resilient economy that creates good jobs and retains more
economic value within the country. Our farmers, growers, and food producers need
reliable access to overseas markets, and securing that access is a core function of
trade policy. What we will not do is trade away the right to regulate in exchange for it.

6. Fair and Managed Trade
The Alliance supports managed and fair international trade, rather than the
ideological pursuit of unrestricted free trade.
Trade policy should be negotiated according to New Zealand's national interests and
democratic priorities.
International agreements must be assessed against their effects on:
- employment;
- wages;
- public services;
- economic sovereignty;

3

---

- environmental protection;
- regional development;
- domestic industry;
- consumer interests.

New Zealand should be free to withdraw from or renegotiate trade arrangements that
substantially undermine these interests.
In government, the Alliance would commission a public review of New Zealand's
existing agreements, including the CPTPP and RCEP, against the tests set out
above, with the findings published and debated in parliament rather than settled in
cabinet.

7. Te Tiriti o Waitangi and Trade Agreements
Every New Zealand free trade agreement since 2001 has included a Treaty of
Waitangi exception clause, intended to preserve the Crown's ability to meet its
obligations to Māori.
The adequacy of that clause has been contested, including in hearings brought to
the Waitangi Tribunal. It has never been tested in a dispute, it was drafted by the
Crown without Māori at the table, and it protects the Crown's freedom to act rather
than Māori rights themselves.
The Alliance will not negotiate trade agreements affecting Māori interests without
Māori participation in the negotiation itself, and will review any exception clause with
Māori to ensure it upholds the mana of Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

8. Buying Local and Government Procurement
Alliance policy commits the state to preferring local materials and local labour in
public construction, and to rebuilding domestic industrial capability.
New Zealand's procurement commitments under the World Trade Organisation
Agreement on Government Procurement, and under the free trade agreements that
build on it, do not prevent this.
Those commitments apply to a defined schedule of entities: the public service
departments, New Zealand Police, the Defence Force, and ten named Crown
agents. Sub-central government is not covered at all. Procurement by state-owned
enterprises, by KiwiRail, and by regional and local government sits outside the
agreements entirely, as do public health, education, welfare, and research services.
Coverage begins at roughly $260,000 for goods and services and roughly $10 million
for construction.
Kāinga Ora is not a covered entity. Neither is any new public construction agency
established outside the public service. The state can therefore prefer New Zealand
materials and New Zealand labour across the great majority of the building

4

---

programme set out in Alliance housing policy without breaching any agreement New
Zealand has signed.
Domestic preference is already government policy in a limited form. The Government
Procurement Rules require agencies to seek economic benefit to New Zealand
above $100,000 for goods and services and $9 million for new construction and
expect contracts below those thresholds to go to capable New Zealand businesses.
The Alliance will strengthen and extend that requirement rather than invent it.
Where coverage does bite, on major departmental contracts above thresholds, we
will pursue the carve-outs needed to apply domestic preference.

Our Trade Vision
The Alliance believes New Zealand should be open to the world without being
owned by the world.
We will support international trade that creates jobs, raises living standards,
develops productive industries, and strengthens relationships with other countries.
We will reject trade arrangements that require New Zealand to surrender democratic
control over our economy, public services, environment, or working conditions.
Trade should be a means to build a stronger country, not an end in itself.

5

# Alliance Transport Policy 2026 (PDF)

> Archive note: Uploaded 2026-09-12; linked from the matching policy post. Text extracted from the party's PDF with pdftotext; bullets normalised to Markdown, page breaks shown as horizontal rules; images/graphics not reproduced.

## Full text (verbatim)

Alliance Party of Aotearoa New Zealand

Transport Policy
A Public Transport System for People, Communities, and the
Environment
Transport is essential public infrastructure. It underpins economic participation,
community wellbeing, and national resilience during climate emergencies and global
disruption.
The Alliance will establish a 100 percent publicly owned, integrated freight and
passenger network in which coastal shipping and rail serve as the twin backbones of
domestic long-distance freight.

1. Public Ownership of Strategic Transport Assets
The Alliance will return and retain strategic transport assets under full public
ownership and democratic control, operating them for social, economic, and
environmental benefit rather than private profit.
- Rail: the national network, tracks, signalling, rolling stock, and intermodal
freight terminals.
- Ports: all sea port infrastructure, with privatisation and contracting out
prohibited.
- Aviation and transit: Air New Zealand, moving from majority Crown control to
full public ownership, together with strategic urban and regional public
transport systems.
- Shipping: a newly established State Shipping Line.
These assets will operate as public services, serving our economic, social, and
environmental needs rather than maximising returns.

2. Rail and Coastal Shipping as Freight Backbones
Rail and coastal shipping will be the primary long-distance freight carriers, shifting
heavy cargo off the highways and reducing emissions, road damage, and deaths.
- Intermodal freight: coordinated schedules and seamless transfer across rail
corridors, ports, and coastal shipping.
- Feeder roading: road freight repositioned as the local, regional, and last-mile
network.

1

---

- Regional access: upgraded heavy-freight links connecting regional productive
sectors directly to national networks.

Freight does not move to rail on its own, because the cost of heavy road transport
falls on the public rather than on the operator and the government will use
legislation, regulation, and investment to correct that.

3. A State Shipping Line
Aotearoa New Zealand no longer has a domestic merchant fleet. The last locally
flagged and crewed container ship left the coastal trade in 2026, the last locally
crewed coastal cement carrier had gone months earlier, and neither was replaced.
There is no longer a domestic drydock able to service a vessel of that size.
We will establish a state-owned shipping line to rebuild domestic maritime capability
and supply chain resilience.
- Scheduled and reliable services: regular coastal, trans-Tasman, and
Pacific regional container and bulk routes.
- Fuel security: restore dedicated domestic coastal fuel tankers.
- Emergency resilience: fund an ocean-going emergency salvage tug and
ensure vessels are available to service isolated regions during civil
emergencies.
- Workforce development: domestic vessels flagged here, crewed under
national collective agreements, and equipped with funded training berths
for cadets.
- Maintenance capability: invest in drydock facilities so that a locally flagged
ship does not have to leave the country for servicing.

4. KiwiPort: A National Port Network
We will replace destructive and parochial port competition with KiwiPort, a nationally
coordinated, publicly owned hub-and-spoke network.
- Hub-and-spoke model: several primary deep-water international hubs,
connected to regional spoke ports by regular domestic coastal feeders.
- Capital rationalisation: an end to the duplication of infrastructure between
competing regional ports.
- Public ownership: port assets retained under shared municipal, regional, and
national public control.

5. Cabotage and Supply Chain Strategy
2

---

We already have cabotage. Section 198 of the Maritime Transport Act 1994 reserves
coastal cargo for Aotearoa New Zealand ships, and for foreign ships on demise
charter to a locally based operator who employs the crew under our law. It also
permits a foreign ship on a continuous international voyage to carry coastal cargo
where that carriage is incidental to its international journey.
That third category now carries the majority of our coastal freight. The exception has
become the rule, and it is why no operator will supply a locally flagged vessel. A ship
paying New Zealand wages competes for the same cargo against vessels crewed on
flag-of-convenience terms, for which the coastal leg is marginal revenue on a voyage
already paid for.
The Alliance will:
- close the incidental-carriage exception in section 198(1)(c), ending the
open-coast policy and reserving domestic sea freight for locally flagged and
crewed ships;
- tighten the ministerial authorisation power in section 198(2);
- require KiwiRail and other state-owned enterprises to use locally flagged and
crewed vessels for coastal freight;
- establish a Sea Freight Group, a ministerial council uniting government, cargo
owners, KiwiPort, and the maritime unions, to drive modal shift;
- ensure seafarers on our coastal and trans-Tasman services are covered by
New Zealand or Australian employment standards, not flag-of-convenience
conditions.

Cabotage governs who may carry coastal freight. It cannot require anyone to send
freight by sea, and it cannot produce a vessel where no operator will provide one.
That is why the law and the fleet must be rebuilt together.

6. Public Transport
The Alliance will establish a fully integrated, quality public transport system covering
urban and regional Aotearoa New Zealand.
- Integrated ticketing, timetables, and network planning across modes and
regions;
- Affordable and, over time, free public transport;
- Restored and expanded regional and long-distance passenger rail;
- Reliable services in smaller centres and rural communities, not only in the
main cities.

3

---

We will repeal the procurement requirements that force public transport into
competitive tendering and corporatised operating models, and allow councils to run
services directly where that delivers better outcomes.
A greater share of fuel excise and road-user charges will be directed towards public
and regional transport.

7. Active Transport and Urban Planning
- Prioritise capital spending on electrified public transit, passenger rail, coastal
shipping, walking, and cycling.
- Build separated, safe cycleway and pedestrian networks for everyday travel.
- Design town planning around accessible public transit rather than private
vehicle movement and parking.

The objective is to give people a real choice. In much of the country there is currently
no alternative to the car, and until there is, reducing car use is not a policy but a
wish.

8. Safety and Worker Protections
- Direct funding towards evidence-based road and transit safety, speed
management, and safer infrastructure design.
- Enforce strict health and safety standards and fair working conditions across
port, rail, road, and maritime operations, using the Approved Code of Practice
for Port Operations as the model.

Transport workers will have safe conditions and enforceable employment
protections. Driver fatigue is a road safety issue as much as an employment one.

9. Accessibility and Partnership
Transport will be fully funded, affordable, and accessible for low-income households,
disabled people, young people, older people, and rural communities.
Accessibility will be built into transport planning from the start rather than added
afterwards.
Transport planning will be undertaken in partnership with iwi and hapū, whose
interests in the network are those of a Te Tiriti partner rather than of a user group.

4

---

10. A National Transport Strategy
We will replace ad-hoc highway spending with a National Transport Strategy
assessing projects on decarbonisation, regional employment, resilience, and
whole-of-life public cost.
We should not have a transport system in which rail competes against roads, buses
compete against trains, ports compete against rail, and local councils compete
against central government for funding.

The Integrated Modal Network
Each mode has a role in a single network rather than a share of a market.
- Coastal shipping: primary domestic bulk and container freight between ports.
- Rail: primary long-distance land freight and inter-regional passenger transport.

- Roads: local, regional feeder, and last-mile freight and vehicle connections.

- Public transit: comprehensive urban, regional, and rural passenger services.

- Active transport: protected walking and cycling routes for short journeys.

- Aviation: publicly owned links between regions and global networks.

A transport system should be judged on affordability, accessibility, regional
resilience, freight efficiency, emissions reduction, and democratic public control. Not
on how many lane-kilometres were opened.

5
