# Alliance Universal Child Benefit and Child Poverty Policy 2026 (PDF)

> Archive note: Uploaded 2026-09-24; linked from the matching policy post. Text extracted from the party's PDF with pdftotext; bullets normalised to Markdown, page breaks shown as horizontal rules; images/graphics not reproduced.

## Full text (verbatim)

Alliance Party of Aotearoa New Zealand

Universal Child Benefit and Child Poverty
Policy
Children, Families, and a Universal Child Benefit
The Alliance believes that every child should have the opportunity to grow up
healthy, secure, and free from poverty.
Children should not be disadvantaged because of the income, employment status, or
circumstances of their parents or carers. Raising children is both a private
responsibility and a contribution to the future wellbeing of the whole society.
The Alliance therefore regards the elimination of child poverty as a primary goal
of government.
Our approach combines universal social provision with targeted assistance where
additional needs exist. We believe that a universal payment to families with children
provides a strong foundation for a fair and effective system of family support.

1. A Universal Child Benefit
The Alliance will establish a Universal Child Benefit, paid for every child in
Aotearoa.
The benefit will be:
- universal, so that every child qualifies regardless of family income;
- paid in respect of each child, recognising the costs associated with raising
children;
- paid directly to the child's primary carer, recognising the unpaid work
involved in caring for children;
- separate from the general welfare benefit system; and
- regularly adjusted to maintain its value over time.
The Universal Child Benefit will provide a guaranteed contribution towards the cost
of raising every child.
Universality is important because children should have an equal social entitlement
regardless of the circumstances into which they are born.
It also ensures that families are not faced with sudden losses of support as their
income changes.

1

---

2. Recognising the Value of Caring Work
The Alliance recognises that raising children involves substantial unpaid work.
Much of this work has historically been performed within families without financial
recognition, despite its enormous contribution to society and the economy.
The Universal Child Benefit will therefore be paid directly to the child's carer.
This recognises that caring for children is socially valuable work, and that families
should receive support for the costs of providing that care.
The policy also reflects the principle that the wellbeing and development of children
is a collective social responsibility.

3. Adequate and Indexed Support
The original NewLabour policy established an important principle: family support
should not simply be introduced and then allowed to lose value through inflation.
The Alliance will therefore ensure that the Universal Child Benefit is regularly
indexed, with the objective of maintaining and improving its real value.
Indexation will be linked to whichever is greater of the Consumer Price Index or
movements in average weekly earnings, ensuring that support for families keeps
pace with broader improvements in living standards, rather than progressively falling
behind.
The benefit should be reviewed periodically to ensure that it remains adequate to
meet the costs of raising children.

4. Universal Provision and the Welfare System
The Universal Child Benefit will remain distinct from general income-support
benefits.
The Alliance supports a strong and comprehensive welfare state in which people
who are unemployed, sick, disabled, caring for others, or otherwise unable to secure
an adequate income receive appropriate support.
The Universal Child Benefit is not intended to replace these forms of assistance.
Rather, it recognises the additional costs associated with raising children and
provides a universal foundation upon which other forms of social security can be
built.
Families with greater needs will continue to be eligible for additional assistance
through the wider social welfare system.

2

---

5. Ending Child Poverty
Universal Child Benefit will form part of a broader Alliance strategy to eliminate child
poverty.
The Alliance will ensure that families have access to:
- adequate incomes;
- affordable and secure housing;
- quality health care;
- accessible early childhood education;
- free and high-quality public education;
- affordable childcare;
- adequate nutrition;
- secure employment and decent wages; and
- comprehensive social security.
The objective is not simply to reduce the number of children below an arbitrary
poverty line. It is to ensure that every child has the material security and
opportunities necessary to participate fully in society.

6. Supporting Working and Non-Working Families
The Universal Child Benefit will be available regardless of whether a child's parents
or carers are in paid employment.
Families should not have to choose between employment and receiving adequate
support for their children.
The policy recognises that families contribute to society in many different ways: —
through paid employment, unpaid caring work, community participation, and the
raising of children.
A universal benefit avoids creating unnecessary divisions between working families
and families receiving other forms of social assistance.

7. Children as Citizens
The Alliance believes that children are not simply dependants of adults. They are
members of our society with their own rights and interests.
Government policy should therefore be assessed according to its impact on children.
The Universal Child Benefit represents a practical expression of this principle: every
child has a claim upon the collective resources of society.

3

---

The state has a responsibility to ensure that no child is denied a decent standard of
living due to circumstances beyond their control.

8. A Foundation for Social Justice
The Universal Child Benefit reflects a broader Alliance principle: social security
should be based on solidarity rather than stigma.
Universal provision creates a shared social entitlement and recognises that everyone
benefits from raising healthy, educated, and secure children.
It also helps redistribute resources towards families at the stage of life when the
costs of supporting children are greatest.
The Alliance will therefore maintain the Universal Child Benefit as a central element
of a comprehensive system of social security.

9. Our Commitment
The Alliance will establish a Universal Child Benefit for every child, paid directly to
their primary carer and regularly indexed to average weekly earnings.
It will remain separate from general welfare benefits and will form the foundation of a
wider programme to eliminate child poverty and improve the wellbeing of children
and families.
We believe that:
- Every child deserves security.
- Every family deserves support.
- Caring for children is valuable work.
- No child should grow up in poverty.
The Universal Child Benefit is a practical expression of our commitment to building a
society in which the wellbeing of children is recognised as a responsibility shared by
us all.

4

documents/pdf-welfare-family-social-secu.title: Alliance Welfare Family and Social Security Policy 2026 (PDF)
documents/pdf-welfare-family-social-secu.text:
# Alliance Welfare Family and Social Security Policy 2026 (PDF)

> Archive note: Uploaded 2026-09-14; linked from the matching policy post. Text extracted from the party's PDF with pdftotext; bullets normalised to Markdown, page breaks shown as horizontal rules; images/graphics not reproduced.

## Full text (verbatim)

Alliance Party of Aotearoa New Zealand

Welfare, Family, and Social Security Policy
A Welfare System Based on Security, Dignity, and Universal
Entitlement
Our Vision
The Alliance believes that every person has the right to a secure and dignified
standard of living. Social security should provide genuine protection against poverty,
illness, disability, unemployment, and the caring responsibilities that arise throughout
people's lives.
Our welfare system should be based on universal rights, adequate incomes,
social solidarity, and respect for human dignity. It should support people when
they need assistance rather than subjecting them to punitive conditions, intrusive
administration, or unnecessary hardship.
The Alliance will build a simpler, fairer, and more comprehensive social security
system that recognises both paid and unpaid work and ensures that no child, family,
student, disabled person, unemployed worker or carer is left without an adequate
income.

1. Universal Family and Child Benefits
Children should have a secure start in life, and families should not be pushed into
poverty because of the costs of raising children.
The Alliance will establish a comprehensive system of universal family payments:
- Universal Early Years Benefit: A universal payment for every child under
three, recognising that the early years of a child's life are fundamental to their
long-term wellbeing and development.
- Universal Child Benefit: A regular, non-means-tested payment for every
child from age three until they turn sixteen. This will provide families with
direct assistance towards the rising cost of raising children.
Universal child and family benefits will be available regardless of family income or
relationship status.

1

---

2. A Simplified and Adequate Social Security System
The present welfare system is unnecessarily complicated, fragmented, and often
punitive. The Alliance will replace the existing collection of overlapping benefit
categories with a simpler and more coherent social security system.
We will:
- establish a Universal Benefit as the foundation of the welfare system, set at
a level that reflects reasonable average living costs and provides a genuinely
adequate standard of living;
- ensure that people receiving social security are treated with dignity and
respect;
- remove unnecessary distinctions between people based on relationship
status;
- individualise benefit entitlements so that a person's access to social security
does not depend on the income or circumstances of their partner;
- replace the current high-compliance welfare model with a high-trust
approach based on support rather than punishment.

Ending Punitive Welfare Practices
The Alliance will abolish benefit sanctions and other punitive measures that push
people further into poverty.
We will:
- abolish benefit sanctions;
- abolish unnecessary stand-down periods, including the six-month stand-down
period for unemployment assistance;
- end the use of welfare debt and debt-recovery practices that trap people in
long-term poverty;
- replace recoverable assistance for urgent needs with grants where
appropriate;
- write off existing beneficiary debt owed to the Ministry of Social Development;
- ban attachment orders against beneficiaries.
The purpose of social security should be to provide security and opportunity, not to
punish people for needing assistance.

2

---

Protecting Incomes Against Inflation
Social security payments must not continually lose their value as the cost of living
rises.
The Alliance will introduce mandatory quarterly indexation of core social
security payments, with increases linked to either average weekly earnings or the
Consumer Price Index, whichever provides the greater increase.
This will ensure that people dependent upon social security do not experience a
gradual erosion of their living standards.

3. Disability, Illness, and Carer Support
People who are unable to work because of illness or disability have the same right to
economic security and dignity as everyone else.
The Alliance will establish comprehensive income and social support for people
living with illness or disability.
Support will:
- provide an adequate income for people unable to work;
- meet disability-related living and medical costs;
- be easily accessible and delivered in a timely manner;
- be available independently of relationship status;
- be available regardless of the cause or origin of the disability.
The social security system should recognise that disability can impose substantial
additional costs and that an adequate income must take those costs into account.

Recognising Unpaid Carers
People who provide substantial unpaid care for children, disabled people, older
people, or family members make an essential contribution to society and the
economy.
The Alliance will establish direct payments to family members and other primary
carers who provide significant unpaid care.
We will develop a caregiver wage to recognise the economic and social value of
unpaid caregiving and to ensure that people are not forced into poverty because they
have taken on essential caring responsibilities.

A Comprehensive Accident and Illness Support System
The Alliance supports extending the principles of comprehensive accident
compensation so that people receive appropriate income support and treatment

3

---

when they experience injury, illness, or disability, regardless of whether the condition
arose from an accident or sickness.
No person should be left without adequate income or necessary treatment simply
because their illness or disability falls outside the circumstances covered by existing
systems.

4. Students and Young People
Education and training should not require young people to live in poverty.
The Alliance will establish a universal student income for people undertaking
tertiary education, vocational education, or training.
The student income will:
- be available universally to eligible students and trainees;
- be set at a liveable level equivalent to the unemployment benefit;
- be independent of parental income;
- provide students with the economic security necessary to participate fully in
education and training.
No young person should be forced to choose between obtaining an education and
being able to afford food, housing, and other necessities.

5. Principles of Alliance Social Security Policy
The Alliance's social security system will be based on five fundamental principles:
1. Universality: essential social security should be understood as a right of
citizenship rather than a source of stigma.
2. Adequacy: payments must provide a genuinely decent standard of living.
3. Dignity: people receiving assistance should be treated with respect rather
than suspicion or punishment.
4. Recognition of Unpaid Work: caring and domestic work are socially and
economically valuable and must be properly recognised.
5. Social Solidarity: society has a collective responsibility to ensure that people
are protected against poverty, unemployment, illness, disability, and other
circumstances beyond their control.
The Alliance believes that a strong social security system is not simply a safety net.
It is an essential part of a fair society in which everyone has the security and
opportunity to participate fully in economic, political, social, and community life.

4

# Women, Gender Equality, and Economic Security (PDF)

> Archive note: Uploaded 2026-09-16; linked from the matching policy post. Text extracted from the party's PDF with pdftotext; bullets normalised to Markdown, page breaks shown as horizontal rules; images/graphics not reproduced.

## Full text (verbatim)

Alliance Party of Aotearoa New Zealand

Women, Gender Equality, and Economic
Security
Our Vision
The Alliance believes that women’s equality is fundamental to a democratic, fair, and
socially just society.

Women cannot achieve genuine equality simply through formal legal rights. Equality
requires action to remove the economic, social, and institutional structures that
continue to disadvantage women. This means addressing discrimination in
employment, unequal pay, poverty, unpaid caring work, violence, inadequate access to
healthcare and reproductive rights, and the barriers that prevent women from
participating fully in public and economic life.

We reject the idea that these inequalities can be left to the market to resolve. The state
has a responsibility to ensure that women have the economic security, freedom, safety,
and opportunities necessary to exercise their rights and participate equally in society.

The Alliance will pursue a comprehensive programme for substantive gender equality,
recognising inequality is experienced differently according to income, class, ethnicity,
disability, age, sexual orientation, family circumstances, and other factors.

1. Equality and Systemic Change
The Alliance will place gender equality at the centre of government policy and decision-
making.

We will:

- require the Government to assess the gender impact of legislation, government
programmes, public expenditure, and major investments before decisions are
made;

- establish a Gender Audit framework to identify and address the effects of
government policies;

- ensure that gender equality is incorporated into economic, employment,
housing, health, education, and social policy;

- address the concentration of women in low-paid, insecure, and undervalued
occupations;

- remove institutional and structural discrimination against women;

1

---

- ensure that public services are accessible and responsive to the different needs
of women;

- give particular attention to women who experience multiple or compounded
forms of disadvantage.

The Alliance recognises the particular rights and circumstances of wāhine Māori, and
will advance gender equality consistently with Te Tiriti o Waitangi and the obligations of
the Crown.

We will also address the specific barriers faced by Pasifika women, women with
disabilities, lesbian women, older women, trans women, migrant women, and women
experiencing poverty or insecure housing.

2. Bodily Autonomy and Reproductive Rights
Every woman has the right to control her own body and make her own decisions about
reproduction.

Reproductive healthcare is a fundamental health right and must not be treated as a
criminal matter.

The Alliance will:

- ensure free, safe, and accessible abortion services throughout Aotearoa;

- remove unnecessary legal, financial, and geographic barriers to abortion;

- ensure access to high-quality, confidential, and non-coercive reproductive
healthcare and counselling;

- provide universal access to contraception through the public health system;

- ensure access to appropriate reproductive and sexual health services
regardless of income, age, disability, or location;

- provide comprehensive, age-appropriate sexuality education in schools,
including education about consent, relationships, health, and bodily autonomy;

- ensure women have access to the information and healthcare necessary to
make informed reproductive choices.

- support an informed consent model of gender-affirming care.

No woman's economic circumstances, geographical location, or relationship status
should determine whether she can exercise control over her own reproductive life.

2

---

3. Recognising Unpaid Work and the Caring Economy
The Alliance recognises that unpaid caring, domestic, and community work makes an
essential contribution to the wellbeing and wealth of Aotearoa.

Women continue to carry a disproportionate share of this work. This contributes
directly to women's lower incomes, reduced retirement savings, interrupted careers,
and economic insecurity.

The Alliance will recognise caring as economically and socially valuable work.

We will:

- establish a Universal Child Benefit for every child, paid directly to the principal
caregiver and indexed to movements in average weekly earnings;

- ensure that support for children is universal rather than dependent upon narrow
means-testing;

- recognise the economic contribution of unpaid caring and domestic work in
national economic and social measures;

- develop measures of national wellbeing that recognise unpaid social and
community contributions alongside conventional economic indicators;

- ensure that carers are not forced into poverty because they undertake essential
unpaid work;

- strengthen public services that support families and carers.

The Universal Child Benefit will recognise that raising children is both a private
responsibility and a contribution to the future of society.

4. Equal Pay and Economic Equality
Women must receive equal pay for work of equal value.

The Alliance rejects the assumption that existing market wages are necessarily fair or
neutral. Historical patterns of discrimination have contributed to the systematic
undervaluing of occupations in which women are concentrated.

We will establish a comprehensive programme of employment and pay equity.

This will include:

- strengthened Employment Equity legislation;

- mechanisms for workers to pursue collective and class-based claims where
discrimination is systemic;

3

---

- a Pay Equity Bureau with responsibility for monitoring and enforcing pay equity;

- comparisons between female-dominated and male-dominated occupations to
determine equal value;

- powers to require employers to provide appropriate pay and employment
information;

- measures to improve wage transparency;

- effective enforcement mechanisms where employers fail to meet pay equity
obligations;

- equal access to education, training, and career progression;

- measures to prevent discrimination in recruitment, promotion, and
employment.

The Alliance will also support policies that increase wages and improve conditions in
traditionally female-dominated occupations, recognising that improving women's
economic position requires action on both discrimination and low pay.

5. Work, Family, and Caring Responsibilities
Having children or caring for family members should never result in economic
disadvantage.

The Alliance will make work and family life compatible by ensuring that responsibility
for caring is shared between individuals, employers, and the state.

Paid Parental Leave
We will provide at least 52 weeks of paid parental leave, available to all eligible
workers, including casual, seasonal and part-time workers.

Parental leave arrangements will recognise that caring responsibilities are not limited to
mothers and will support parents and caregivers to share caring responsibilities.

Employment Protections
We will strengthen the Employment Relations Act to require employers to act in good
faith in accommodating legitimate family and caring responsibilities.

Workers should be able to seek flexible working arrangements without being
disadvantaged because they have children or other caring responsibilities.

Childcare
The Alliance will establish a comprehensive, accessible, and affordable system of high-
quality childcare.
4

---

This will include support for non-profit and publicly supported childcare services,
including services capable of meeting the needs of people working outside
conventional hours.

We recognise that many workers are employed in shifts, evenings, nights, and
weekends. Childcare provision must reflect the reality of working life rather than
assume that every family operates from 9 am to 5 pm.

Older Persons’ Care
With an ageing population, unpaid care work includes more and more support for older
family members and friends, including peer support.

The Alliance Party will improve retirement provisions, increase funding for aged care
and support, and establish and fund independent advocacy services for older
people.
We believe the whole of society benefits when older people are able to live with as
much dignity and security as anyone else, meaning that the support they need to
thrive should be undertaken by society as a whole.

A Shorter Working Week
The Alliance supports a progressive reduction in standard working hours, including the
movement towards a 35-hour working week, without loss of income.

A shorter working week would help redistribute unpaid domestic labour, improve work-
life balance and allow women and men to participate more equally in paid
employment, family life, and community life.

6. Ending Violence Against Women
Every woman has the right to live free from violence, intimidation, and abuse.

Violence against women is not simply an individual problem. It is a major social and
public health issue requiring sustained government action.

The Alliance will:

- invest in comprehensive prevention programmes addressing the underlying
causes of violence;

- provide education about healthy relationships, consent, equality, and non-
violence;

- ensure adequate long-term public funding for women's refuges and specialist
support services;

5

---

- end competitive short-term funding arrangements that undermine the stability of
essential services;

- provide secure, non-contestable funding for organisations providing essential
protection and support;

- ensure women fleeing violence have access to safe and affordable housing;

- strengthen the enforcement of protection orders;

- ensure police, courts, and other agencies have the resources necessary to
respond effectively to family and sexual violence;

- ensure children are properly protected from violence and abuse;

- support and provide funding for kaupapa Māori informed models for addressing
harm;

- provide appropriate support for survivors and their children.

Protection orders and other legal protections must be backed by the resources
necessary to make them effective. A legal right is of little value if the state cannot
provide the practical protection required to enforce it.

7. Women, Poverty, and Economic Security
Women are disproportionately affected by poverty, low wages, insecure employment,
and inadequate retirement income.

The Alliance will address the economic causes of women's disadvantage through a
combination of decent wages, secure employment, adequate income support,
affordable housing, universal public services, and recognition of unpaid caring work.

We will:

- support full employment and secure, properly paid work;

- ensure social security provides an adequate standard of living;

- improve support for sole parents and families;

- ensure that women are not forced into poverty because of caring
responsibilities;

- strengthen women's access to affordable housing;

- protect and improve public health, education, childcare, and social services;

- address the long-term retirement income consequences of unpaid caring and
interrupted employment.

6

---

Women's economic independence is essential to their ability to exercise genuine
freedom and equality.

8. Women's Participation and Representation
Women must have an equal voice in the institutions that govern and shape society.

The Alliance will promote women's participation and leadership across government,
Parliament, public services, workplaces, and community organisations.

We will:

- remove barriers to women's participation in public and political life;

- promote equal representation in decision-making;

- support women's leadership and participation in traditionally male-dominated
sectors;

- address discrimination and harassment that prevent women from participating
fully;

- ensure government decision-making reflects the diversity of women in Aotearoa.

9. A Commitment to Substantive Equality
The Alliance believes that equality means more than treating everyone identically.

A genuinely equal society must address the different circumstances and barriers
experienced by different groups of women.

Our policies will therefore recognise the particular experiences of:

- wāhine Māori;

- Pasifika women;

- women with disabilities;

- lesbian women;

- trans women;

- older women;

- women experiencing poverty;

- women in insecure or low-paid work;

- sole parents;

- migrant and refugee women;

7

---

- women experiencing violence and homelessness.

We will ensure that gender policy is developed in partnership with the women and
communities directly affected.

Conclusion
Women's equality is not an optional addition to social policy. It is fundamental to the
kind of society the Alliance Party seeks to build.

The Alliance will pursue a society in which women have genuine economic
independence, control over their own bodies, equal pay, secure employment, access
to affordable childcare, adequate income, freedom from violence, and an equal voice
in the decisions that affect their lives.

We will recognise the value of paid and unpaid work, strengthen the public services on
which families depend, and challenge the structural inequalities that have historically
limited women's freedom and economic security.

The Alliance is committed to a society in which all women are free, secure,
economically independent and equal participants in the life of Aotearoa New
Zealand.

8

# Alliance Workers’ Rights and Employment Policy 2026 (PDF)

> Archive note: Uploaded 2026-09-07; linked from the matching policy post. Text extracted from the party's PDF with pdftotext; bullets normalised to Markdown, page breaks shown as horizontal rules; images/graphics not reproduced.

## Full text (verbatim)

Alliance Party of Aotearoa New Zealand

Workers' Rights and Employment Policy
Decent Work, Fair Wages, and Democratic Workplaces
The Alliance believes that secure, fairly paid, meaningful work is a basic human
right.
A prosperous society should not depend upon low wages, insecure employment, or
the weakening of workers’ rights. Every person who works should be able to earn a
decent living, work in a safe environment, spend time with their family, and
participate meaningfully in decisions affecting their workplace.
The Alliance rejects the idea that workers’ wages and conditions should be treated
simply as costs to be minimised in a competitive labour market.
We will rebuild the bargaining power of working people, strengthen trade unions,
establish decent minimum standards, and give workers a genuine voice in the
management and direction of their workplaces.

1. Work Is a Basic Right
Every person has the right to the opportunity for meaningful, secure, and fairly paid
employment.
The Alliance will pursue full employment as a central economic objective.
Where the private economy fails to provide sufficient employment, the government
will directly intervene through publicly funded apprenticeship, employment, and
infrastructure programmes.
These programmes will provide useful work in areas including:
- infrastructure;
- housing;
- environmental restoration;
- conservation;
- community services;
- public transport;
- regional development.

Unemployment should not be treated as an inevitable feature of the economy.
A government committed to full employment must be prepared to create work where
the market fails to do so.

1

---

2. A 35-Hour Working Week
The Alliance will establish a 35-hour standard working week without loss of earnings.
The 35-hour week will be accompanied by appropriate protections to ensure that
employers cannot simply increase work intensity or use unpaid overtime to
circumvent the reduction in hours.
Workers will have:
- a statutory right to refuse unreasonable hours or shifts;
- mandatory penal rates for overtime;
- proper payment for all hours worked;
- protection from pressure to work excessive hours.

Reducing working hours should improve quality of life, family time, and community
participation while allowing the benefits of increased productivity to be shared with
workers.

3. Five Weeks' Paid Annual Leave
The Alliance will guarantee a minimum of five weeks’ paid annual leave for all
workers.
Annual leave is not simply a workplace benefit. It is essential to health, family life,
and the ability of workers to participate fully in their communities.

4. Paid Parental and Family Leave
Workers should not have to choose between employment and their responsibilities to
their families.
The Alliance will provide 52 weeks of paid parental leave, available to all workers,
including:
- part-time workers;
- casual workers;
- seasonal workers.

The Alliance will also establish paid compassionate leave for workers who need to
attend funerals, tangi, or deal with serious family circumstances.
Employment law will require employers to properly recognise and accommodate
workers’ family and whānau responsibilities.
The principle will be simple:
Work should fit around family life, not family life around work.

2

---

5. A Living Wage and Protection Against Inflation
The minimum wage should provide a genuine standard of living rather than simply
represent the minimum amount an employer can legally pay.
The Alliance will immediately increase the adult minimum wage to two-thirds of the
average wage, with the adult minimum applying to workers of all ages.
From there we will establish mechanisms to protect workers’ purchasing power from
inflation, including automatic annual wage adjustments linked to movements in the
cost of living. This would include consideration of the consumer price index (CPI)
and average ordinary time hourly earnings from the quarterly employment survey
(QES).
Economic growth should translate into rising living standards for working people.

6. Equal Pay and Pay Equity
Women and other groups of workers have historically been undervalued in the
labour market.
The Alliance supports the re-introduction of comprehensive Pay Equity legislation to
ensure equal pay for work of equal value.
The legislation will:
- allow comparisons across different industries and occupations;
- provide effective mechanisms for collective claims;
- allow workers to pursue class-wide or occupational pay equity claims;
- establish a clear process for resolving claims;
- aim to achieve genuine pay equity within three years.

Pay equity must address not only discrimination between people doing the same job,
but the historical undervaluing of predominantly female occupations.

7. Wage Theft Is Theft
The deliberate underpayment of workers must be treated seriously. Employers who
knowingly steal workers’' wages will face prosecution and meaningful penalties.
Workers should not have to spend years pursuing money they have already earned.

8. Investigation and Prosecution of Breaches
The Alliance Party will support adequate funding and resourcing for bodies tasked
with monitoring and making judicial decisions on Health & Safety, workplace
conditions, breaches of employment law, and worker exploitation.
Namely, we will ensure the Employment Relations Authority is given adequate
resourcing and power so that cases are heard and ruled on in a timely manner. A
new Workplace Safety Authority will be established to hear cases regarding health,
3

---

safety, and wellbeing in the workplace and relieve the backlog of cases from the
Employment Relations Authority. We will also increase the authority and size of the
Labour Inspectorate.
Working people must not wallow in unsafe, unfair, or unlawful conditions for
extended periods of time waiting for justice.

9. Restore Collective Bargaining Power
Individual workers are rarely equal in bargaining power to their employer.
Collective bargaining is therefore essential to achieving fair wages and decent
conditions.
The Alliance will restore and strengthen a coordinated national system of wage
determination, providing minimum standards across industries and occupations.
Collective agreements will provide a floor below which employment conditions
cannot fall.
The Alliance will strengthen the ability of workers to bargain collectively through their
unions and will ensure that employment law supports rather than undermines
collective organisation.

10. A Strong and Democratic Trade Union Movement
Trade unions are fundamental democratic institutions.
The Alliance will protect workers’ rights to:
- join a union;
- form a union;
- organise collectively;
- bargain collectively;
- participate in union activities;
- vote on union membership arrangements;
- receive union assistance at work.

Unions will have the legal right to meet and organise workers in groups during
working hours, subject to reasonable arrangements for the workplace.
Pacific and migrant workers will have access to state-funded, mother-tongue
interpreters where necessary to participate fully in union activities and employment
negotiations.

4

---

11. Restore the Right to Strike
The right to withdraw labour is a fundamental democratic right.
The Alliance will restore a broad right to strike, including protection for:
- industrial action over employment conditions;
- solidarity and sympathy strikes;
- collective action in support of other workers;
- appropriate political strikes.

Workers should not be required to surrender their collective power simply because
they enter employment.
The right to strike is the necessary counterbalance to the power of employers.

12. Workplace Democracy
Workers should have a genuine voice in the decisions that affect their working lives.
The Alliance will legislate for Work Councils in enterprises employing more than fifty
workers.
Work Councils will provide workers with a formal role in decisions concerning:
- workplace organisation;
- health and safety;
- restructuring;
- training;
- technological change;
- employment conditions;
- major changes affecting the workforce.

In enterprises employing more than 250 workers, workers will have the right to elect
Worker Directors to the governing board.
This will begin the transformation of workplaces from institutions where workers
simply receive instructions into institutions in which workers have a genuine
democratic voice.

13. Protect Workers During Restructuring
Workers should not be treated as disposable whenever a company experiences
financial difficulties or decides to restructure.
Where significant redundancies are proposed, employers will be required to:
- provide workers and their representatives with relevant financial
information;
5

---

- negotiate alternatives to redundancy with unions;
- provide at least one month’s notice of dismissal;
- genuinely examine alternatives to job losses;
- consider redeployment and retraining.

Where a business is facing serious financial difficulty, workers and their
representatives should have access to sufficient information to participate
meaningfully in determining its future.

14. A National Retraining and Redeployment Programme
Where technological change, restructuring, or economic circumstances make jobs
genuinely redundant, workers should not simply be left unemployed.
The Alliance will establish state-funded retraining, redeployment, and relocation
programmes.
These programmes will help affected workers move into:
- new occupations;
- growing industries;
- essential public services;
- regional employment opportunities;
- further education and vocational training.

A dedicated employer contribution or levy will help fund the programme.
The costs of economic restructuring should not be carried solely by the workers who
lose their jobs.

15. Protect Precarious and Vulnerable Workers
Workers in insecure employment are particularly vulnerable to exploitation.
The Alliance will establish a comprehensive Minimum Employment Code covering
workers who are currently vulnerable because they are:
- non-unionised;
- employed through agencies;
- contractors;
- casual workers;
- seasonal workers;
- in other precarious forms of employment.

6

---

Employment status must not be used as a mechanism for avoiding basic
employment rights.

The Alliance will ensure that workers performing essentially the same work receive
comparable minimum protections regardless of the contractual structure used by
their employer.

16. Regulate Contracting and Labour Hire
Employers should not be able to undermine wages and conditions simply by
replacing permanent employees with contractors or labour-hire workers.
The Alliance will strengthen regulation of:
- labour-hire companies;
- contracting arrangements;
- dependent contractors;
- casual employment;
- outsourcing.

Where contracting is used primarily to avoid employment obligations, workers will be
entitled to appropriate protections.
The objective is to ensure that employment status cannot become a loophole for
exploitation.
17. Work, Childcare and Community Life
A decent employment system must recognise that workers have lives outside the
workplace.
The Alliance will establish non-profit, community-based 24-hour childcare, jointly
funded by government and employers, to support workers whose employment
requires non-standard hours.
This will particularly assist:
- shift workers;
- night workers;
- healthcare workers;
- transport workers;
- emergency workers;
- hospitality and service workers;
- single parents.

7

---

Childcare should be treated as essential social infrastructure supporting both families
and the economy.

8

---

18. Health and Safety at Work
Every worker has the right to return home safely at the end of the working day.
The Alliance will restore and maintain strong statutory health and safety protections
and ensure that workers and their unions have a meaningful role in workplace safety.
Employers will be required to provide safe workplaces, appropriate training, and
adequate resources to manage workplace risks.
Workers will have effective rights to raise safety concerns without fear of retaliation.
Health and safety representatives and unions will be supported in monitoring
workplace safety.

19. Workers’ Rights and Economic Policy
Workers’ rights cannot be separated from wider economic policy.
The Alliance will pursue an economic system based on:
- full employment;
- rising real wages;
- strong collective bargaining;
- public investment;
- productive industry;
- regional development;
- worker participation;
- economic security.

We reject the concept of "labour market flexibility" when it is used to mean weaker
wages, insecure work, fewer rights, and the transfer of economic risk from employers
to workers.
Flexibility should work for workers as well as employers.

9

---

Our Vision for Work in Aotearoa New Zealand
The Alliance believes that a decent society should guarantee that people who work
can live with dignity.
We will build an employment system in which:
- work provides a living wage;
- employment is secure;
- hours are reasonable;
- families have time together;
- workers receive proper leave;
- women receive equal pay for work of equal value;
- unions have genuine power;
- workers have a voice in their workplaces;
- redundancy does not mean abandonment;
- and no worker is exploited because of their employment status.

The Alliance’s objective is not simply to improve employment law.
It is to rebalance economic power between employers and workers.
A productive economy should benefit the people who create its wealth. The people
who work in our workplaces must have a fair share of that wealth, a genuine voice in
its distribution, and democratic rights over the conditions under which they work.

10

# We are back to fight for working people in 2026

## Full text (verbatim)

The Alliance Party has welcomed the announcement of the 2026 General Election date of 7 November, saying that it is ready to offer New Zealanders a genuine social democratic alternative to the failed policies of the status quo.

Alliance Party President Victor Billot says the return of the Alliance comes at a critical time as working people are being crushed by a cost-of-living crisis.

This Government has waged war on the majority while rolling out the red carpet for the already wealthy and powerful, he says.

“We have seen a sustained attack on public services, an ongoing housing crisis, and stagnating wages and jobs. It is a government of the rich, for the rich, that shows contempt for the needs of the working people who are the backbone of New Zealand.”

Mr Billot says the Alliance provides a voice for those who have been abandoned by the long-term shift to the right in New Zealand politics.

“We are seeing record profits for overseas-owned banks and supermarket duopolies while families struggle to put food on the table. The political establishment – both the anti-worker Government and a timid and compromised Opposition – refuses to challenge the economic structures that create this inequality.”

“The Alliance is not afraid to say that the system is broken, and we are not afraid to offer real solutions.”

The Alliance is campaigning on bold, practical solutions to the cost-of-living crisis, including:

- Tax Justice: Tax reform to take the tax burden off the working majority and a wealth tax to ensure the super-rich pay their fair share to keep the country running.
- Public Ownership: Halting asset sales and taking back control of our energy, transport and infrastructure to serve people, not private profit.
- Housing for All: A massive investment in state housing.
- Free Public Services: Free healthcare and education, funded by a fair tax system.

“We don’t need tinkering, we need transformation,” says Mr Billot.

“The Alliance is bringing an unapologetic message back to the electorate. New Zealand can be a country where everyone has enough, where our environment is protected, and where the economy operates in the service of the community.”

The Alliance will officially launch its campaign and manifesto at its National Conference in Christchurch on 14 February 2026.

The Party confirmed it will be standing electorate candidates in key seats across the country, ensuring that voters have the chance to cast a vote for real change.

“We invite every New Zealander who is tired of their future being sold out to join us.”

# Alliance Party prepares for 2026 General Election campaign at Conference

The Alliance Party will be working on its campaign for the 2026 General Election this Saturday 14 February at its National Conference in Christchurch.

Members from across Aotearoa will gather at the Trade Union Centre to ratify the party’s constitution, elect national officers, and confirm the policy platform for the upcoming election.

Alliance Party President Victor Billot says the conference marks a pivotal moment for the political left in New Zealand.

“The Alliance is back to offer a genuine social democratic alternative to the failed policies of the status quo,” says Mr Billot.

“We are seeing record profits for overseas-owned banks and supermarket duopolies while families struggle to pay the bills. # Alliance Calls for Universal Child Benefit

## Full text (verbatim)

The Alliance Party says current economic and social pressures highlight the need for meaningful cost-of-living relief and stronger support for young families, regardless of their background or employment status.

Alliance Party social welfare spokesperson and West Coast–Tasman candidate Sara Dyatlova-Murphy says many families are delaying having children, or having fewer children, because of the rising cost of living.

> “Families should not have to choose between having children and being able to afford the basics. We need a system that provides reliable support to all families raising children,” Ms Dyatlova-Murphy says.

The Alliance supports the Child Poverty Action Group’s (CPAG) call to examine Working for Families and the In-Work Tax Credit.

> “Targeted approaches such as these have created a two-tier system that can leave some of the families who need support the most without assistance,” Ms Dyatlova-Murphy says.

Families can miss out on the In-Work Tax Credit if they receive a main benefit or student allowance, or if they do not work enough hours. Families can also face unexpected overpayment bills when estimated weekly or fortnightly payments are reconciled at the end of the financial year.

> “Working for Families and the In-Work Tax Credit are failing too many New Zealand families. Means testing creates unnecessary administrative costs and complexity, while support has not kept pace adequately with wages or done enough to reduce child poverty.”

The Alliance is campaigning to restore the Universal Child Benefit, with regular payments made to the main caregiver to help meet the costs of raising children.

> “A universal payment would remove much of the complexity and administrative burden of the current system. It would give families less stress, greater dignity and greater financial security, allowing parents and caregivers to focus on raising happy, healthy children,” Ms Dyatlova-Murphy says.

The Alliance has also supported an immediate increase in all benefits, with regular indexation to average weekly earnings so that support does not fall behind the cost of living and wage growth.

Under the Alliance’s Universal Child Benefit proposal, payments would continue until each child turns 16.

> “Every child deserves a secure start in life, and every family should have the support they need to provide it. A Universal Child Benefit is a simple, fair and effective way to make that happen,” Ms Dyatlova-Murphy says.

# Our Tax Plan Makes First $20,000 Income Tax-Free, Funded by Wealth Tax

## Full text (verbatim)

**Alliance Party Media Release**\
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE\
Sunday 6 September 2026

The Alliance Party has unveiled its tax package, proposing to make the first $20,000 of every person’s income completely tax-free. Under the proposed scale, an everyday worker earning $65,000 would keep an extra $2,408 a year.

## Download the policy documents

- [**Tax Justice and Cost of Living Policy**](https://allianceparty.nz/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/alliance-tax-justice-cost-of-living-policy-2026.pdf)PDF, 4 pages, 135 KB
- [**Tax Policy Costings: The Numbers**](https://allianceparty.nz/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/alliance-tax-policy-costings-2026.pdf)PDF, 5 pages, 195 KB

The package combines taxes on wealth, realised capital gains, and financial transactions with a 30% corporate tax rate and a rebalanced income tax scale. The Alliance’s costings estimate a net revenue surplus in both the first term and at year 10.

- **$20,000 Tax-Free Threshold:** Universal, automatic, and permanent relief. All earners below the $178,150 break-even point pay less income tax. Proposed upper rates are 34% from $78,100 to $150,000; 39% from $150,000 to $250,000; and 47% above $250,000.
- **2.5% Wealth Tax:** An annual tax on individual net wealth above $2 million, estimated to raise $6.59 billion annually. A couple pays nothing on combined net wealth up to $4 million. A companion trust tax is estimated to raise a further $0.11 billion.
- **33% Capital Gains Tax:** Applies to realised gains accruing after the tax begins, fully excluding the family home. Estimated annual revenue rises from a first-term average of $0.54 billion to $2.22 billion at year 10.
- **Financial Transactions Levy:** A 0.1% levy covering equity and onshore foreign exchange turnover, estimated to raise $0.64 billion annually. Everyday household payments, wages, bills, and KiwiSaver contributions are strictly exempt.

Alliance Finance and Economy Spokesperson Quentin Findlay says the central focus of the policy is taxing wealth, not work.

> “Aotearoa New Zealand currently taxes income from the very first dollar earned, while untaxed wealth multiplies without effort.
>
> “The Alliance is offering a completely different set of priorities to provide working people and their families with security in a cost-of-living crisis.
>
> “By shifting the tax burden onto those who already hold extensive wealth, an essential worker on $65,000 keeps an extra $2,408 every year. This is about ensuring our economy serves the people who actually do the work.”

**ENDS**

For more information contact Alliance Party Finance and Economy Spokesperson Quentin Findlay on Mobile [021 326 443](tel:+6421326443)

# Full Employment and a 35-Hour Week in Our Workers’ Rights Policy

## Full text (verbatim)

**Alliance Party Media Release**\
Monday, 7 September 2026, 7:58 am

The Alliance Party has released its policy for employment relations and workers’ rights.

## Read the full policy

**Workers’ Rights and Employment Policy**\
PDF, 10 pages, 195 KB

[Download policy PDF](https://allianceparty.nz/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/alliance-workers-rights-employment-policy-2026.pdf)\

Alliance employment relations spokesperson and candidate for Selwyn, Jesse Luke, says the policy is “pro-worker, pro-union, and pro-jobs.”

“Working people must be able to protect and advance their interests collectively. For 40 years trade unions and workers’ rights have been under attack, driving a race to the bottom in our wages and conditions.”

He says the Alliance policy includes full employment, a 35-hour working week with no loss in pay, five weeks of annual leave, workplace democracy, and a broad restoration of the right to strike.

“Currently, the employer holds the purse strings and the worker sells their labour to them. To have a fair go, workers need the right to withdraw their labour.”

“No one takes such action lightly, and a loss of pay is a significant sacrifice, but New Zealand has highly restrictive strike laws. The Alliance will change that.”

Mr Luke says the policy sets the Alliance apart because it is not simply about improving wages and conditions, but about rebalancing economic power between employers and workers.

“The Alliance does not accept workplaces being run like dictatorships when people spend such a large part of their lives at work. Workers have a genuine interest in the successful and fair operation of their workplaces, and they deserve a real say in the decisions that affect them.”

The Alliance policy proposes Work Councils in workplaces with more than 50 workers and elected Worker Directors in enterprises employing more than 250 workers.

The Alliance policy includes greater support and resourcing of the Employment Relations Authority and the Labour Inspectorate, alongside establishing a Workplace Safety Authority.

“Exploitation, breaches of employment law, and dangerous workplace practices will be taken seriously. We will treat wage theft as theft. We will advance legislation for corporate homicide and corporate manslaughter.”

“There must be no more deaths on the waterfront, in forestry, and in other high-risk industries. Employers that breach employment and workplace safety law must face effective enforcement and meaningful penalties.”

# Public Power, Clean Water, Polluters Pay: A Just Transition in Our Environment Policy

## Full text (verbatim)

The Alliance Party says Aotearoa New Zealand should stop treating economic growth as the main measure of national progress, and instead judge government policy by whether it improves people’s lives while protecting the environment.

The proposal is at the core of the Alliance’s new Environmental, Climate, and Sustainable Economy Policy, which sets out a vision for a “cooperative, ecological economy”.

## Read the full policy

Environmental, Climate, and Sustainable Economy Policy\
PDF, 11 pages, 211 KB

[Download policy PDF](https://allianceparty.nz/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/alliance-environment-climate-sustainable-economy-policy-2026.pdf)

Alliance environment spokesperson and Christchurch Central candidate Greg Byrnes says environmental and economic policy can no longer be treated as separate issues.

> “An economy can be growing on paper while natural resources are depleted, ecosystems are damaged, and communities carry the wider costs,” says Mr Byrnes.

“We need to ask whether people are better off, and are we leaving a healthy environment for future generations?”

The Alliance proposes moving towards a Genuine Progress Index, or GPI, as a central measure of national progress, alongside environmental auditing and true-cost accounting.

The GPI would take account of environmental health, public health and wellbeing, social equality, economic security, public services, unpaid caring and community work, and the interests of future generations.

Mr Byrnes says government decisions need to be judged on their real social and environmental consequences, not simply on whether they increase Gross Domestic Product (GDP).

The policy also proposes:

- a polluter-pays principle requiring those responsible for environmental damage to meet the full cost of prevention and repair;
- the “right to repair” and a move towards a zero-waste, circular economy;
- 100 percent public ownership of electricity generation, transmission, distribution, and retail with a focus on renewables;
- replacing the Emissions Trading Scheme with a carbon tax, with revenue directed towards renewable energy, public transport, and emissions reduction;
- keeping water infrastructure and services in public ownership, with stronger controls on water pollution; and
- prohibiting mining in national parks, conservation areas, and other protected public land.

Mr Byrnes says deteriorating freshwater quality including rivers and groundwater shows why urgent environmental action is necessary.

He says environmental change must not come at the expense of workers and communities.

“We know parts of our economy still depend on finite and extractive resources, but multinational corporations cannot be trusted to look after either the environment or their workers when those industries reach the end of the road.”

“As part of a Just Transition, the government must retrain and redeploy workers, invest in alternative industries and support communities affected by change.”

The Alliance proposes bringing extractive industries into public ownership as they are progressively wound down, with revenue used for environmental restoration, worker retraining, redeployment, and regional investment.

Mr Byrnes says the basic principle of the Alliance policy is straightforward.

“Our economy must serve people and communities, and it has to operate within the ecological limits of the planet.”

For more information, contact Alliance Environment Spokesperson and Christchurch Central candidate Greg Byrnes on mobile 021 0245 5398

## About Greg Byrnes

Mr Byrnes is a former regional councillor on [Environment Canterbury](https://www.ecan.govt.nz/) (2022–2025), and was chair of the Regional Biodiversity & Biosecurity Committee during 2023.

He is a professional environmentalist and spent twelve years as general manager of Tūhaitara Coastal Park, a 750 ha coastal wetland and dune area in North Canterbury.

Alliance environment spokesperson and candidate for [Christchurch Central](https://allianceparty.nz/candidates/christchurch-central/).

# Our Health Policy Eliminates Costs for GP Visits, Dental, Optical, and Audiology Services

## Full text (verbatim)

The Alliance Party has announced its health policy, which includes the elimination of costs for GP visits, dental, optical, and audiology services.

[Download the full health policy (PDF, 7 pages) ↓](/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/alliance-health-policy-2026.pdf)

In order to achieve this, the policy creates the Community Health Service (CHS) as the main funding and logistical service to bring primary and allied health services into the public service.

Existing services have the option to join the CHS, with the CHS covering the costs of the practice, including rent, payroll, administration, and information technology. The staff would be employed by the CHS.

For the patients, there would be very few changes in the short term. The CHS would take over the practice, but the patients would still see the same doctors, and it would still be the same clinic. The biggest change would be that appointments would be free.

The CHS would also change how the system is funded. Primary care funding moves beyond capitation, with money allocated for things like chronic care clinics. Community and hospital services would then be funded as one system, so that keeping someone out of hospital counts as a win rather than a hospital losing the funding for treating them.

Alliance health spokesperson and candidate for Christchurch East, Ethan Gullery, says this is a positive step towards a fully integrated health care system.

> “Right now, we treat the system as a bunch of disconnected pieces, funding hospitals one way and funding clinics another. We know that the best care is earliest care, but the focus is on the secondary care system. The Alliance wants to change that.”

In the Alliance's CHS model, community and primary care workers would be equal to their secondary care colleagues in pay and would come under the existing collective agreements. Māori health providers would keep the option to remain independent, with full funding and pay equity for their staff either way.

> “A fragmented system means a fragmented workforce, negotiating with many employers, trying to get the bare minimum.”

Mr Gullery says this change is the shakeup needed.

> “We have heard from GPs and GP practices, and it has become obvious in those conversations that very few people become doctors in order to end up being small businesspeople. Not only that but they are running small businesses in an area where the economics stopped being favourable decades ago. The Alliance is the only party willing to stand up and say the entire system needs to change.”

# Our National Strategy on Transport

## Full text (verbatim)

The Alliance Party has announced its transport policy focused on delivering economic participation, community wellbeing, and national supply chain resilience during climate emergencies and global disruption.

[Download the full transport policy (PDF, 5 pages) ↓](/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/alliance-transport-policy-2026.pdf)

The Alliance will establish a 100-percent publicly owned, integrated freight and passenger network in which coastal shipping and rail serve as the twin backbones of domestic long-distance freight.

The Alliance is committed to public ownership of other strategic transport assets such as ports, aviation and transit.

Alliance Party transport spokesperson and candidate for Banks Peninsula, Kyle Turnbull, says New Zealand cannot keep relying on road freight domestically, or on global shipping companies for exporting and importing.

> “New Zealand is a remote island nation and a relatively small market on the global stage. An integrated and efficient transport system for moving goods domestically and internationally is essential for our economic sovereignty and national security.”

Mr Turnbull says recent disruptions to global supply chains have already shown that New Zealand is exposed and vulnerable.

> “Whether the threat is the closure of a key shipping lane such as the Strait of Hormuz, a global pandemic, or extreme weather events, New Zealand needs resilient supply chains.”
>
> “By setting up rail and coastal shipping as the twin backbones of freight, we will build a resilient network that can respond to natural disasters, reduce carbon emissions, and move freight off roads.”

In the maritime transport sector, Alliance would establish a State shipping line as part of a wider domestic and regional shipping plan, and implement a national port strategy.

The Alliance proposes an increase in funding for public transport, and the repeal of procurement requirements that force local government into corporatised models of public transport provision.

Mr Turnbull says public transport works the best when it is well run, properly funded, and affordable, so that people from all walks of life use it as the first choice for their daily commute.

> “That means it needs to be run as a public service, integrated nationally, and made as widely available as possible – not just in the cities but also in the regions – so people can get where they need to go.”
>
> “Our upgrade of commuter rail across the country will provide jobs and reconnect regional New Zealand and small towns to the wider economy.”
>
> “The neglect of our regions is evident in the lack of infrastructure, and the absence of a plan for regional economic development. It is a decades-long scandal. The Alliance is committed to changing that, and our transport policy will form a key part of that change.”

For more information contact Alliance Party transport spokesperson and [candidate for Banks Peninsula Kyle Turnbull](/candidates/banks-peninsula/) on [0224685436](tel:+64224685436).

# Our Plan to Rebuild Universal Social Security

## Full text (verbatim)

The Alliance Party will end benefit sanctions, individualise social security entitlements, and establish a Universal Benefit as the foundation of a new social security system under its 2026 election policy.

[Download the full welfare, family and social security policy (PDF, 4 pages) ↓](/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/alliance-welfare-family-social-security-policy-2026.pdf)

The Alliance will also introduce universal payments for children and families, end unnecessary benefit stand-down periods, and replace the current high-compliance welfare model with a high-trust system based on adequate incomes, dignity, and universal entitlement.

Alliance social security spokesperson and West Coast–Tasman candidate Sara Dyatlova–Murphy said the policy represented a fundamental change in how New Zealand treats people who need income support.

> “Social security must stop people falling into poverty, not punish them once they get there.
>
> “Losing a job, becoming ill or disabled, caring for a family member, or needing help while studying are ordinary risks and responsibilities. We need to ensure people have security when those things happen.”

The Universal Benefit would be set at a level reflecting reasonable average living costs and providing an adequate standard of living.

Entitlements would be individualised, so a person’s access to support would no longer depend on their partner’s income or circumstances.

Ms Dyatlova–Murphy said the Alliance would also abolish sanctions, unnecessary stand-down periods, and welfare debt and debt-recovery practices that push people further into hardship.

> “Taking money away from someone who already cannot afford food, rent, or power does not solve unemployment or poverty. It simply makes a bad situation worse.”

The policy would write off existing beneficiary debt owed to the Ministry of Social Development and replace recoverable assistance for urgent needs with grants where appropriate.

Core social security payments would be indexed quarterly to either average weekly earnings or the Consumer Price Index, whichever produced the greater increase.

Families would receive a Universal Early Years Benefit for every child under three, followed by a Universal Child Benefit from age three until sixteen, regardless of family income or relationship status.

> “Universal child support recognises that helping families raise healthy, secure children is a responsibility shared across society,” Ms Dyatlova–Murphy says.

The policy would also expand support for people living with illness or disability, provide direct payments for family members and other primary carers, and develop a caregiver wage recognising the value of unpaid care.

Students and trainees would receive a universal student income, independent of parental income and set at a liveable level equivalent to the unemployment benefit.

> “Everyone should have the security to participate fully in their family, their community, and society, whatever their circumstances.”

For more information contact Alliance Party Social Security spokesperson and [West Coast–Tasman candidate Sara Dyatlova–Murphy](/candidates/west-coast-tasman/) on [022 4147223](tel:+64224147223).

# 52 Weeks’ Paid Parental Leave in Our Gender Equality Plan

## Full text (verbatim)

The Alliance Party has announced a comprehensive women, gender equality, and economic security policy including at least fifty-two weeks’ paid parental leave, a Universal Child Benefit, and stronger enforcement of pay equity.

[Download the full Women, Gender Equality, and Economic Security policy (PDF, 8 pages)](/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/alliance-women-gender-equality-economic-security-policy-2026.pdf)

Alliance Party national secretary and gender equality spokesperson Sionainn Byrnes says formal rights alone cannot overcome the barriers that prevent many women from participating fully in society.

> “Legal equality is necessary, but it is not enough. Women need the economic security, public services, and practical support that allow them to exercise their rights and participate fully in society.”

The Alliance policy would provide at least fifty-two weeks’ paid parental leave to eligible workers, including casual, seasonal, and part-time workers. Its parental-leave arrangements would recognise that caring responsibilities are shared by parents and caregivers.

A Universal Child Benefit would be paid directly to the principal caregiver for every child and indexed to movements in average weekly earnings.

Ms Byrnes says care work is economically and socially valuable, and it needs to be treated as such.

> “Raising children and caring for whānau should not push people into poverty, reduce their retirement security, or limit their opportunities at work. Properly recognising care work is non-negotiable.”

The policy would also establish a Pay Equity Bureau to monitor and enforce pay equity. It provides for strengthened Employment Equity legislation, collective and class-based claims where discrimination is systemic, greater wage transparency, and comparisons between female-dominated and male-dominated occupations to assess work of equal value.

Ms Byrnes says women remain concentrated in work that has been undervalued and underpaid.

> “People working in care and support roles, and other female-dominated occupations, deserve proper recognition and fair pay.”

The Alliance would support accessible, affordable, and high-quality childcare, including non-profit and publicly supported services for parents working shifts, evenings, nights, and weekends.

The policy also affirms bodily autonomy and reproductive healthcare. It supports free, safe, and accessible abortion services throughout Aotearoa, universal access to contraception through the public health system, comprehensive age-appropriate sexuality education, and an informed consent model of gender-affirming care.

Other commitments include secure, long-term funding for women’s refuges and specialist services, safe and affordable housing for women fleeing violence, gender-impact assessments of government decisions, and progressive movement towards a thirty-five-hour working week without loss of income.

Ms Byrnes says the policy recognises the particular rights and circumstances of wāhine Māori under Te Tiriti o Waitangi, as well as the different barriers experienced by Pasifika women, disabled women, older women, migrant women, lesbian and trans women, sole parents, and women facing poverty or insecure housing.

> “Women’s equality must mean economic independence, control over our own bodies, freedom from violence, and an equal voice in the decisions that shape our lives.”

For more information contact Alliance Party national secretary and gender equality spokesperson Sionainn Byrnes on [022 060 6549](tel:+64220606549)

# Small Is Beautiful! Backing Small Business, Local Enterprise, and Cooperatives

## Full text (verbatim)

[The Alliance Party](https://allianceparty.nz/) has announced its Small Business, Local Enterprise, and Cooperative Development policy, with a strategy to protect independent operators, raise working standards, and curb the dominance of corporate monopolies.

[Download the full Small Business, Local Enterprise, and Cooperative Development policy (PDF, 6 pages)](https://allianceparty.nz/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/alliance-small-business-local-enterprise-cooperative-policy-2026.pdf)

Alliance Party small business spokesperson Anna Knight says New Zealand’s small businesses, family farms, independent contractors, and cooperatives are essential to a democratic, resilient economy.

> “Small businesses keep wealth in local circulation and communities sustained but are currently bearing the brunt of an unfair economic system.”

Ms Knight says small businesses suffer from a race to the bottom when it comes to wages, hours, and conditions, both for their workers, and for owner-operators who are under immense pressure.

The policy launch follows a spike in insolvencies, with 2025 company liquidations reaching levels not seen since the aftermath of the 2010 Global Financial Crisis.

About half of New Zealand’s small businesses close within five years, and fewer than thirty percent survive a decade.

> “Insolvency doesn’t happen overnight, the so-called ‘failure curve’ creeps up and is the result of many forces. We want to attack these at the root.”

> “We want to reset this dynamic and ensure everyone in a small enterprise gets a fair deal.”

Ms Knight says to reverse this trend, the Alliance will restructure the tax base so the burden falls on concentrated, accumulated wealth rather than productive small enterprises.

The Alliance will overhaul competition law to break up corporate market power, with a focus on sectors like the supermarket duopoly, which extracts an estimated $430 million annually in excess profits. Suppliers can’t negotiate easily with just two buyers, and small retailers simply can’t compete.

A publicly owned development bank will be established to deliver low-cost financing for local enterprise, backed by community resource hubs and an Applied Technology Programme to foster domestic tech sovereignty.

The Alliance will create a framework to support employee buy-outs with targeted development in regional economies.

Minimum employment protections will be extended to contractors to stop wage undercutting, alongside mandatory maximum payment terms and public reporting on payment times for large corporate buyers.

Ms Knight says it is important to remember that all wage-earning is essentially a credit given to your employer, and, by the same token, a small business should not be providing an interest-free loan to a company many times its size.

> “Our goal is not simply to grow business balance sheets, but to decentralise economic power so it directly serves local communities, workers, and families.”

For more information contact Alliance small business spokesperson Anna Knight on [02040728703](tel:+642040728703)

# Justice Policy: “Three Strikes and into Treatment”

## Full text (verbatim)

The Alliance Party has released its 2026 Justice Policy, built around preventing harm, repairing it, and standing with victims.

[Download the full Justice Policy (PDF, 8 pages)](https://allianceparty.nz/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/alliance-justice-policy-2026.pdf)

Alliance Party justice spokesperson and Ilam candidate Courtney Fraser says the state of the courts and prisons is not an accident but a policy choice.

> “It’s hard to talk about criminal justice without talking about policy, because where we find ourselves today with incarceration, the lack of rehabilitation, and the lack of access to services, is down to public policy.”

> “Our criminal law is still built around punishing the people who offend, and there is far too little for the victims of crime.”

> “Underinvestment in housing, work, training, and education over the last forty years has led to a social crisis, and our courts are where that crisis ends up.”

Ms Fraser says the Alliance policy tackles the causes of offending through secure housing, decent work, education and training, healthcare, and mental health and addiction services.

The policy establishes habilitation centres as an alternative to prison, particularly for young people, and brings back Community Care Orders as a sentencing option.

It places restorative justice at the centre of appropriate responses to offending, supports marae-based processes where appropriate, and properly resources iwi and Māori organisations to provide rehabilitation and restorative programmes.

A properly resourced Victim/Criminal Compensation Board will oversee financial, physical and other support for victims of crime.

Ms Fraser says the Alliance will review legal aid with the aim of a comprehensive, publicly funded system of legal assistance, including expanded legal aid, sustainable resourcing for Community Law Centres, and an enhanced Public Defence Service, so that no one is denied justice because they are poor.

Prisons will be publicly owned and operated, and the Alliance opposes private prisons. Reflecting its principle that no person or corporation is above the law, the Alliance will also reinstate the right to sue corporations or individuals over damage caused by emissions-related climate change effects.

> “We’re all in this together on these tiny, faraway islands. We must close the gaps in our systems so none of us are left behind.”

> “The best thing we can do for victims is stop making new ones. Where the current approach is three strikes and out, ours is three strikes and into treatment.”

The policy rests on six principles: prevent rather than simply punish; rehabilitate rather than abandon; restore where possible rather than simply incarcerate; support victims rather than abandoning them; guarantee access to justice regardless of wealth; and protect rights by holding everyone, including government and corporations, accountable under the law.

For more information, contact Alliance Party justice spokesperson and Ilam candidate Courtney Fraser on [027 470 8900](tel:+64274708900)

# Alliance Party Plan to Eliminate Child Poverty

## Full text (verbatim)

The Alliance Party has further elaborated on its social security and welfare policies, with a focus on the elimination of child poverty.

[Download the full policy (PDF, 4 pages) ↓](https://allianceparty.nz/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/alliance-universal-child-benefit-and-child-poverty-policy-2026.pdf)

Alliance social security spokesperson and West Coast-Tasman candidate Sara Dyatlova Murphy said the policy provides greater detail on the previously announced Universal Child Benefit, with a broader social justice focus.

> “No child should grow up in poverty in Aotearoa New Zealand, and the fact is that children are not being paid poverty benefits or poverty wages – that happens to their caregivers” Ms Dyatlova-Murphy said.

The Alliance policy emphasises the status of children as citizens in their own right, not merely the dependants of adults. Ms Dyatlova-Murphy said all government policy must consider the impact on children as members of our society with their own rights and interests.

“The same level of care given to the impact on women, on the environment, on tangata whenua, when auditing government policy should also apply to some of the most vulnerable in our community who can not directly impact government through voting – children and youth.”

Ms Dyatlova-Murphy says the policy has been shaped by the work of the Child Poverty Action Group, whose research has kept child poverty on the national agenda for more than thirty years.

“CPAG have spent decades documenting what poverty does to children in this country, and making the case for change when it wasn’t popular. Their work has shaped our thinking, and we’re grateful for it.”

CPAG’s 2026 election manifesto challenges every party to commit to solutions for children. The Alliance policy is our answer to that challenge.

> “There is no reason a child in this country should grow up in poverty and insecurity. Children have a claim over the shared resources of our society, and until all children are provided with what they need to thrive we will never realise our full potential as a nation.”

“If we care for the next generation, every New Zealander will benefit.”

For more information contact Alliance Party Social Security spokesperson and [West Coast – Tasman candidate Sara Dyatlova–Murphy](/candidates/west-coast-tasman/) on [022 4147223](tel:+64224147223)
